No. It places an image of your signature on the page. Documents that legally need a certificate-based digital signature require a DSC or Aadhaar eSign from a licensed provider.

**Can I add my signature to every page?**
Yes. Select the placed signature or initials and turn on **On every page**. It appears in the same spot on all pages.

**Is my signature stored or uploaded?**
No. It is never uploaded. It stays in this browser tab, and is saved on your device only if you turn on **Remember on this device**.

**Can someone remove my signature from the PDF?**
Someone with a PDF editor could. To make the page harder to change, flatten the PDF or turn it into images after signing, and keep a copy of what you sent.

## JSON to XML Converter

URL: https://justtools.online/developer-tools/json-to-xml/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-05

Convert JSON to XML online: attributes, text, arrays and nested data, with a root element, CDATA and pretty or minified output. Free and private, no upload.

### At a glance

- Keys starting with **@** become attributes and **#text** becomes element text — the same convention as the XML to JSON converter, so data round-trips.
- Arrays can **repeat the element** (`<tag>a</tag><tag>b</tag>`) or **wrap each item** (`<tags><item>a</item>…</tags>`), and nested arrays always produce valid XML.
- Data without a single root is wrapped in a **root element** you can name; top-level arrays get one item element per entry.
- Keys that aren’t valid XML names are fixed (“first name” → `first_name`, “2nd” → `_2nd`) and listed, and characters XML can’t hold are removed and reported.
- Options for the XML declaration, **CDATA** sections, self-closing empty elements and 2-space, 4-space, tab or minified output.
- Accepts relaxed JSON (comments, trailing commas, single quotes) and points to the exact line and column of real errors. Big numbers keep every digit.
- Runs entirely in your browser — the JSON is never uploaded.

### Features

- **Attributes and text**: Write `{"price": {"@currency": "INR", "#text": "799"}}` and get `<price currency="INR">799</price>` — exactly what most XML APIs expect.
- **Your array style**: Repeat the element for each entry, or wrap entries in item elements — whichever the receiving system wants.
- **Always valid XML**: Invalid names are fixed, special characters escaped, mixed content kept on one line and empty arrays handled, with a note for every change.
- **Round-trips**: Switch to XML → JSON at any time: the result converts straight back, so you can edit data as JSON and send it as XML.
- **Exact numbers**: IDs and amounts like 12345678901234567890 or 1.50 are written exactly as in the JSON, never rounded.
- **Private**: API payloads and configs stay on your device. No upload, no sign-up.

### How to convert JSON to XML

1. **Paste the JSON** — Paste JSON into the left box, open a .json file, or try the **Sample**.
2. **Set the options** — Open **Options** to choose the root and item element names, how arrays are written, CDATA and the XML declaration.
3. **Check the result** — The XML appears as you type, with notes about anything that was renamed, wrapped or removed.
4. **Copy or download** — Click **Copy**, or **Download** to save an .xml file.

### Guide

#### How JSON maps to XML

| JSON | XML |
| --- | --- |
| `{"user": {"name": "Asha"}}` | `<user><name>Asha</name></user>` |
| `{"user": {"@id": "7"}}` | `<user id="7"/>` |
| `{"price": {"@currency": "INR", "#text": 799}}` | `<price currency="INR">799</price>` |
| `{"list": {"tag": ["a", "b"]}}` | `<list><tag>a</tag><tag>b</tag></list>` (or wrapped: `<list><tag><item>a</item><item>b</item></tag></list>`) |
| `{"note": null}` | `<note/>` |
| `[1, 2]` | `<root><item>1</item><item>2</item></root>` |

#### Good to know

XML has no data types, so numbers, booleans and null all become text: `true` is written as `<paid>true</paid>`. An empty array can’t be shown with repeated elements, so it is left out (with a note) unless you choose **Wrap items**.

Converting the other way? Use the [XML to JSON converter](https://justtools.online/developer-tools/xml-to-json/). To check or tidy JSON first, try the [JSON Formatter](https://justtools.online/developer-tools/json-formatter/).

### FAQ

**How do I convert JSON to XML?**
Paste your JSON into the box. The XML appears on the right straight away — copy it or download it as an .xml file.

**How do I make an XML attribute from JSON?**
Start the key with @. For example `{"book": {"@id": "42", "title": "Gitanjali"}}` becomes `<book id="42"><title>Gitanjali</title></book>`. You can change the prefix under Options.

**How are JSON arrays converted?**
By default each entry repeats the element: `"tag": ["a","b"]` gives two `<tag>` elements. Choose **Wrap items** to get `<tag><item>a</item><item>b</item></tag>` instead, and set the item element’s name.

**Why was my data wrapped in <root>?**
An XML document must have exactly one top-level element. If your JSON has several top-level keys, or is an array, it’s wrapped in a root element — you can rename it under Options.

**Can it convert invalid JSON?**
It accepts common slips — comments, trailing commas, single quotes and unquoted keys — and tells you what it fixed. For real errors it shows the line and column so you can correct them.

**Is my JSON uploaded?**
No. The conversion runs in your browser, so API responses, keys and customer data never leave your device.

## Cron Expression Generator

URL: https://justtools.online/developer-tools/cron-expression-generator/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-05

Build and explain cron expressions in plain English with next run times. Supports Linux crontab, Quartz, Spring and AWS EventBridge, and converts between them.

### At a glance

- Four formats: **Unix / Linux cron** (crontab, Kubernetes, GitHub Actions), **Quartz** (with seconds and year), **Spring @Scheduled** and **AWS EventBridge**.
- Explains any expression in **plain English** — e.g. `30 9 * * 1-5` is “At 9:30 AM, Monday through Friday” — in 12- or 24-hour time.
- Shows the **next 10 run times** in your time zone or UTC, including L, W and # rules, leap years and the Unix “either day” rule.
- **Converts** a schedule between formats, rewriting day-of-week numbers (Sunday is 0 in Unix and Spring but 1 in Quartz and AWS), `?` and seconds — or explains why it can’t.
- Errors point to the exact field (“Hour: 24 is out of range (0–23)”), and an expression in the wrong format is recognised and you’re offered a switch.
- Presets and a simple builder for every few minutes or hours, daily, weekly, monthly and yearly schedules, plus ready-to-paste crontab, GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Spring and AWS snippets.
- Warns about schedules that never run (30 February) or skip months, and about day-of-month + day-of-week combinations that run more often than expected.

### Features

- **Plain-English check**: Paste the expression from a crontab, YAML file or code review and read what it actually does before it ships.
- **Real next runs**: See the next ten dates and times — “in 3 h 15 min” — so a schedule that’s off by a day or an hour is obvious.
- **Every scheduler**: Unix cron, Quartz, Spring and AWS each have their own rules. Pick the one you use and the syntax is checked for it.
- **Convert between them**: Moving a job from crontab to Spring or EventBridge? Get the equivalent expression with day numbers and “?” fixed.
- **Build without memorising**: Choose “Every week”, tick Mon–Fri and pick a time — the expression is written for you.
- **Share a schedule**: Copy a link that opens the tool with your expression and format, for a ticket or code review.

### How to create a cron expression

1. **Pick the format** — Choose **Unix**, **Quartz**, **Spring** or **AWS** — the one your scheduler uses.
2. **Build or paste** — Click a preset, use **Build a schedule**, or paste an expression and edit any field.
3. **Check it** — Read the plain-English description and the **Next runs**; switch between your time zone and UTC.
4. **Copy it** — Copy the expression or a ready-made snippet for crontab, GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, Spring or AWS.

### Guide

#### Cron syntax at a glance

`*` any value · `,` list (1,15) · `-` range (9-17) · `/` step (*/15) · `?` no value · `L` last · `W` nearest weekday · `#` nth weekday (FRI#3).

| Field | Unix | Quartz / Spring | AWS |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Second | — | 0–59 | — |
| Minute | 0–59 | 0–59 | 0–59 |
| Hour | 0–23 | 0–23 | 0–23 |
| Day of month | 1–31 | 1–31, L, W, ? | 1–31, L, W, ? |
| Month | 1–12 or JAN–DEC | 1–12 or JAN–DEC | 1–12 or JAN–DEC |
| Day of week | 0–7 (0 and 7 = Sun) | Quartz 1–7 (1 = Sun) · Spring 0–7, L, # | 1–7 (1 = Sun), L, #, ? |
| Year | — | Quartz only, optional | 1970–2199 |

#### Common cron expressions

| Schedule | Unix cron | Quartz |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Every 5 minutes | `*/5 * * * *` | `0 */5 * * * ?` |
| Every hour | `0 * * * *` | `0 0 * * * ?` |
| Every day at midnight | `0 0 * * *` | `0 0 0 * * ?` |
| Weekdays at 9:30 AM | `30 9 * * 1-5` | `0 30 9 ? * MON-FRI` |
| Every Sunday at 6 PM | `0 18 * * 0` | `0 0 18 ? * SUN` |
| 1st of every month | `0 0 1 * *` | `0 0 0 1 * ?` |
| Last day of the month | not possible | `0 0 0 L * ?` |

#### Things that often go wrong

**Time zones:** cron uses the server’s time zone, GitHub Actions always uses UTC, and EventBridge rules run in UTC. Check the next runs in UTC if your job runs at the “wrong” hour.

**Both day fields in Unix cron:** `0 0 1 * 1` runs on the 1st **and** every Monday, not only on Mondays that are the 1st.

**Day numbers:** Monday is 1 in Unix and Spring but 2 in Quartz and AWS. Using names like MON avoids mistakes.

### FAQ

**How do I run a cron job every 5 minutes?**
Use `*/5 * * * *` in Unix cron. In Quartz it’s `0 */5 * * * ?`, in Spring `0 */5 * * * *` and in AWS `*/5 * * * ? *`.

**What does * * * * * mean?**
Every minute. The five fields are minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week; * means “every”.

**What is the difference between Unix cron and Quartz cron?**
Quartz adds a seconds field at the start (and an optional year), numbers days of the week 1–7 starting with Sunday, needs a “?” in either day-of-month or day-of-week, and supports L, W and #. The tool converts between them.

**How do I schedule a job on the last day of the month?**
Use L in day-of-month in Quartz, Spring or AWS, e.g. `0 0 0 L * ?`. Standard Unix cron has no last-day option; a common workaround is to run daily on days 28–31 and check the date in the script.

**Why does my GitHub Actions schedule run at a different time?**
GitHub Actions cron is always in UTC (and may start a few minutes late when busy). India is UTC+5:30, so 9:00 AM IST is `30 3 * * *`. Switch Next runs to UTC to check.

**Can cron run every 30 seconds?**
Not standard Unix cron — its smallest unit is a minute. Quartz and Spring have a seconds field: `*/30 * * * * ?` (Quartz) or `*/30 * * * * *` (Spring).

## CSS to Tailwind Converter

URL: https://justtools.online/developer-tools/css-to-tailwind/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-05

Convert CSS to Tailwind classes online: hover, media queries, dark mode and gradients become variants, colours match the palette. Tailwind v4 and v3, free.

### At a glance

- Outputs **Tailwind v4** classes by default, or **v3** — scales, colour names and syntax differ (for example `p-3.25` and `shadow-sm` in v4 vs `p-[13px]` and `shadow` in v3).
- `:hover`, `:focus`, `::before`, `:first-child`, `[aria-expanded="true"]`, `@media (min-width: 768px)`, dark mode and `@supports` become **variants** like `hover:`, `before:`, `first:`, `aria-expanded:`, `md:`, `dark:` and `supports-[…]:`.
- `.card:hover .title` becomes `group-hover:` (adding `group` to `.card`) and `input:checked + label` becomes `peer-checked:`.
- Colours in hex, rgb(), hsl() or OKLCH are matched to the **Tailwind palette** (v3 hex and v4 colours), with opacity like `bg-black/50`; an option picks the nearest palette colour.
- Shorthands are merged into Tailwind shortcuts: `px-4`, `truncate`, `size-10`, `line-clamp-3`, gradients as `bg-linear-to-r from-… to-…`.
- Anything without an exact class becomes an **arbitrary value** (`p-[13px]`, `[-webkit-text-stroke:1px]`), highlighted so you can review it; close-but-not-identical matches are marked.
- The converter is tested against the real Tailwind v4 compiler, so the classes it writes exist. Runs in your browser — your CSS isn’t uploaded.

### Features

- **Whole stylesheets**: Paste rules, media queries and nested CSS together — classes are grouped by element, with each breakpoint and state in one class list.
- **Exact, not guessed**: 13px stays 13px. Values are only replaced by a Tailwind step when it is exactly the same; otherwise you get an arbitrary value.
- **Honest approximations**: Where Tailwind is close but different — like CSS “ease” vs ease-in-out — the class is marked and the difference explained.
- **Palette matching**: Recognises Tailwind colours from design files, including v4’s OKLCH values, and keeps opacity as /50 modifiers.
- **See where it came from**: Hover a class, or open “How each class was made”, to see the CSS declaration behind it.
- **Ready to paste**: Copy the classes, a class="" attribute or a JSX className for each selector, with your project’s prefix if it uses one.

### How to convert CSS to Tailwind

1. **Paste your CSS** — Paste a rule, a whole stylesheet or a few declarations into the CSS box — or try the **Sample**.
2. **Choose the version** — Pick **Tailwind v4** or **v3**, and set a prefix or nearest-colour matching if you need them.
3. **Review** — Classes appear for each selector. Amber classes are arbitrary values; underlined ones are close, not identical.
4. **Copy** — Copy the classes, a class attribute or a JSX className and paste them into your HTML or components.

### Guide

#### Examples

| CSS | Tailwind v4 |
| --- | --- |
| `display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 8px` | `flex items-center gap-2` |
| `padding: 12px 24px` | `py-3 px-6` |
| `margin: 0 auto; max-width: 768px` | `my-0 mx-auto max-w-3xl` |
| `color: #1e293b; background: rgba(0,0,0,.5)` | `text-slate-800 bg-black/50` |
| `border: 1px solid #e5e7eb; border-radius: 8px` | `border border-gray-200 rounded-lg` |
| `overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; white-space: nowrap` | `truncate` |
| `.btn:hover { background: #1d4ed8 }` | `hover:bg-blue-700` |
| `@media (min-width: 768px) { .a { padding: 32px } }` | `md:p-8` |
| `padding: 13px` | `p-3.25` (v4) · `p-[13px]` (v3) |

#### Tips

Keep **@keyframes** and **@font-face** in your CSS (or in your Tailwind theme) — the converter lists them as skipped and you can use `animate-[…]` and `font-[…]` to refer to them.

In Tailwind v4, `dark:` follows the system setting unless you set up class-based dark mode. Tailwind’s preflight already makes borders solid, so `border-solid` is left out.

### FAQ

**How do I convert CSS to Tailwind?**
Paste your CSS into the box. The tool shows the Tailwind classes for each selector straight away, including hover states and breakpoints — copy them into your HTML.

**Does it support Tailwind v4?**
Yes — v4 is the default. Switch to v3 for older projects; the classes follow each version’s scales and syntax (v4 `p-4!` vs v3 `!p-4` for important, for example).

**Why are some classes like p-[13px]?**
They are arbitrary values: Tailwind has no class for exactly that value (in v3) or it’s not on any scale. They work as-is; you can also switch them to the nearest scale value by hand.

**Will hex colours become Tailwind colour names?**
When they match a Tailwind palette colour exactly — v3 hex values and v4’s colours both count — yes, e.g. #1e293b → slate-800. Turn on **Nearest colours** to use the closest palette colour for the rest.

**Does it convert media queries and :hover?**
Yes. Min-width queries at 640, 768, 1024, 1280 and 1536px become sm:, md:, lg:, xl: and 2xl:; others become min-[…]: or max-[…]:. :hover, :focus, ::before, :first-child, dark mode and more become variants.

**Is my CSS uploaded?**
No. The conversion runs entirely in your browser.

## Hash Generator

URL: https://justtools.online/developer-tools/hash-generator/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-05

Generate MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-512, SHA-3, BLAKE3, CRC32 and HMAC hashes of text or files, and verify checksums. Free, fast and private — no upload.

### At a glance

- 17 algorithms: **MD5, SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA3-256, SHA3-512, Keccak-256, BLAKE2b, BLAKE3, RIPEMD-160, CRC32, CRC32C, Adler-32, xxHash64** and **XXH3**.
- **Files of any size** are read in 2 MB pieces and hashed with every chosen algorithm in one pass, with progress and speed shown.
- **HMAC** with a secret key (text, hex or Base64) for API and webhook signatures, e.g. HMAC-SHA256.
- **Compare** with a hash you were given — hex, Base64, `sha256=…` or SRI format — or paste a whole **SHA256SUMS** list to check several files by name.
- **Each line** mode hashes a list one value at a time (with optional trimming and lowercasing, as ad platforms require for emails) and exports a CSV.
- Output as lowercase hex, uppercase hex or Base64; text input as UTF-8, hex or Base64 bytes.
- Runs entirely in your browser with WebAssembly — nothing you hash is uploaded. Results are checked against the published test vectors.

### Features

- **Verify downloads**: Drop an ISO, installer or APK and paste the checksum from the download page — the tool tells you instantly whether it matches.
- **Many algorithms at once**: See MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512 side by side, or add SHA-3, BLAKE3 and checksums — the file is read only once.
- **Webhook signatures**: Recreate the HMAC-SHA256 of a payload with your secret to debug Razorpay, Stripe, GitHub or Shopify webhooks.
- **Hash a list**: Normalise and hash a column of emails or phone numbers line by line, then download value and hash as CSV.
- **Find the algorithm**: No match? The tool suggests which algorithms produce a hash of that length and adds them with one click.
- **Private**: Passwords, keys and files never leave your device. No upload, no sign-up and no size limit.

### How to generate a hash

1. **Choose what to hash** — Pick **Text**, **Each line** or **Files**, and select the algorithms you need.
2. **Add your data** — Type or paste text, or drop one or more files. Turn on **HMAC** and enter a key for a keyed hash.
3. **Copy the result** — Hashes appear instantly. Choose hex, HEX or Base64 and click the copy button next to any hash.
4. **Verify (optional)** — Paste the expected hash or checksum list into **Compare with a hash** to see whether it matches.

### Guide

#### Which hash should I use?

| Use | Algorithm |
| --- | --- |
| Checking a download, file integrity | SHA-256 (or whatever the publisher lists) |
| API / webhook signatures | HMAC-SHA256 |
| Ethereum addresses and signatures | Keccak-256 (not SHA3-256) |
| Fast deduplication or cache keys | BLAKE3, xxHash64 or XXH3 |
| ZIP, PNG and gzip checksums | CRC32 |
| Old systems that only accept it | MD5 or SHA-1 — never for security |
| Storing passwords | None of these — use bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 with a salt |

#### Checking a file from the command line

To compare with what this tool shows: on Windows run `certutil -hashfile file.iso SHA256` (or `Get-FileHash file.iso` in PowerShell), on macOS `shasum -a 256 file.iso`, and on Linux `sha256sum file.iso`.

Hashing text in a terminal? `echo "hello" | sha256sum` includes a line break at the end — use `echo -n` (or `printf`) to match the tool, which hashes exactly what is in the box.

### FAQ

**How do I generate a SHA-256 hash?**
Type or paste your text into the box — the SHA-256 hash appears instantly along with MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-512. For a file, choose **Files** and drop it in.

**How do I verify a file’s checksum?**
Choose **Files**, drop the file, and paste the checksum from the download page into **Compare with a hash**. A green “Match” means the file is exactly what the publisher released.

**Why doesn’t my hash match?**
Hashes change with every byte. The usual causes are a trailing space or line break, different text encoding, uppercase vs lowercase input, or the wrong algorithm. The tool warns about trailing spaces and suggests algorithms that match the length of your hash.

**Can I reverse or decrypt a hash?**
No. Hashes are one-way: you can’t get the original text back. Sites that “decrypt” MD5 only look the hash up in tables of common passwords.

**Is MD5 still safe to use?**
Not for security — collisions can be made deliberately. It is fine for spotting accidental corruption or where a system requires it. Use SHA-256 or newer for anything security-related.

**Is there a file size limit?**
No. Files are read in small pieces, so even multi-gigabyte files work; the speed depends on your device.

**Is my data uploaded?**
No. All hashing happens in your browser with WebAssembly. Your text, files and secret keys never leave your device.

## Age Calculator

URL: https://justtools.online/calculators/age-calculator/
Category: Calculators
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-05

Calculate your exact age in years, months and days, the next birthday countdown and age on any date. Check exam age limits as on a cut-off date. Free.

### At a glance

- Gives your **exact age in years, months and days**, plus your age in total months, weeks, days, hours, minutes and seconds — live, to the second, with an optional time of birth.
- Shows your **next birthday**: the date, weekday, the age you’ll turn and a countdown, and the **day of the week you were born**.
- Calculates **age on any date** — past or future — not just today.
- **Exam age limit** mode checks your age **as on a cut-off date** (like “1 August”) against a minimum and maximum age, with OBC, SC/ST and PwBD relaxation, and shows the allowed range of birth dates.
- Upper limits can follow the UPSC/SSC wording (“must not have attained 32”) or count completed years; both are shown exactly, day by day.
- **Age difference** mode compares two dates of birth in years, months and days.
- Month lengths and leap years are handled exactly; someone born on 29 February has their birthday on 28 February in other years. Runs in your browser — your date of birth isn’t sent anywhere.

### Features

- **Exact to the day**: Counts calendar months the way birthdays work, so 31 January to 28 February is one month — no 30-day approximations.
- **Exam-ready**: Enter the “age as on” date and limits from a UPSC, SSC, banking or state exam notification and see at once whether you qualify.
- **Birthday countdown**: See how many months and days until your next birthday, the weekday it falls on and the age you’ll turn.
- **Fun milestones**: Find out when you’ll be 10,000 days old, 1,000 weeks or a billion seconds — and how many seconds old you are right now.
- **Any date**: Work out an age on a past or future date: at admission, retirement, a policy date or a wedding.
- **Private**: Calculated on your device. Your date of birth is never uploaded or stored.

### How to calculate your age

1. **Enter your date of birth** — Pick the date in the **Date of birth** box. Add your time of birth for exact hours and seconds (optional).
2. **Choose the date** — The age is worked out for today; change **Age on** to calculate it for any other date.
3. **Read the result** — See your age in years, months and days, your next birthday, and your age in months, weeks, days, hours and seconds.
4. **Check an exam limit (optional)** — Open **Exam age limit**, enter the cut-off date and the minimum and maximum age, and choose any relaxation.

### Guide

#### How exam age limits are worked out

Notifications give an age range and a date, such as “21 to 32 years as on 1 August 2026”. You must have **reached the minimum age** on that date. For the upper limit, UPSC and SSC say you **must not have attained** the maximum age — so with a limit of 32 you must still be 31 on the cut-off date.

That is why such notices list birth dates instead: for 21–32 as on 1 August 2026, a candidate must be born **not earlier than 2 August 1994 and not later than 1 August 2005**. The calculator shows this range for any limits you enter, including relaxation.

| Category | Usual upper age relaxation (central government) |
| --- | --- |
| OBC (non-creamy layer) | 3 years |
| SC / ST | 5 years |
| Persons with Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD) | 10 years (13 for OBC, 15 for SC/ST) |
| Ex-servicemen, J&K domicile and others | Varies — see the notification |

#### Good to know

Age in months and days depends on month lengths, so two people with the same number of days alive can have slightly different “years, months and days”. This calculator counts whole calendar months first, then the remaining days — the same way you count birthdays.

Planning finances by age? The [EMI calculator](https://justtools.online/calculators/emi-calculator/) shows a loan’s monthly payments, and the [BMI calculator](https://justtools.online/calculators/bmi-calculator/) uses your age to explain results for children and teens.

### FAQ

**How do I calculate my exact age?**
Enter your date of birth. The calculator counts the completed years and months since then, and the days left over — for example 26 years, 8 months and 20 days — and shows the same age in total days, weeks and hours.

**How do I calculate my age on a specific date?**
Change the **Age on** date to the date you need, such as an exam cut-off or admission date. The age is worked out for the start of that day.

**Am I eligible for an exam with an age limit “as on 1 August”?**
Open **Exam age limit**, enter your date of birth, 1 August of the exam year, and the minimum and maximum ages from the notification. Add your category’s relaxation. The calculator says whether you’re within the limit and shows the allowed birth dates. The notification is always final.

**What does “must not have attained 32 years” mean?**
You must not have had your 32nd birthday on or before the cut-off date. If you turn 32 on the cut-off date itself, you are not eligible; if you turn 32 the day after, you are.

**How is the age of someone born on 29 February calculated?**
In years without 29 February, this calculator counts the birthday on 28 February, so the person turns a year older then. Some countries use 1 March for legal purposes.

**Is my date of birth saved?**
No. Everything is calculated in your browser and nothing is sent or stored.

## PPK to PEM Converter

URL: https://justtools.online/security-tools/ppk-to-pem/
Category: Security Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-05

Convert a PuTTY .ppk private key to PEM or OpenSSH format online, with or without a passphrase. Supports PPK v2 and v3, RSA, ECDSA and Ed25519. No upload.

### At a glance

- Reads **PuTTY PPK version 2 and 3** files, including passphrase-protected ones (Argon2 for v3, as PuTTY 0.75 and later write them).
- Converts to **PEM** (BEGIN RSA / EC / DSA PRIVATE KEY), **OpenSSH** (BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY), **PKCS#8** or another **PPK** version.
- Supports **RSA, ECDSA (P-256, P-384, P-521), Ed25519** and DSA keys.
- Checks the key file’s MAC, so a wrong passphrase or a damaged file is reported instead of producing a broken key.
- Can add a new passphrase to the converted key, and shows the **SHA256 fingerprint** and public key line (for authorized_keys).
- Tested against keys made by PuTTYgen and checked with OpenSSH’s ssh-keygen and OpenSSL.
- Runs entirely in your browser — the private key is never uploaded.

### Features

- **Without PuTTYgen**: Convert on any computer or phone — no need to install PuTTY or use the command line on a Mac or Linux machine.
- **Passphrases handled**: Unlock an encrypted .ppk with its passphrase, and choose whether the new key has one.
- **Every format**: PEM for AWS and older tools, OpenSSH for modern ssh and Git, PKCS#8 for code libraries.
- **Verify before you use it**: Compare the SHA256 fingerprint with the one your server or PuTTYgen shows.
- **Public key too**: Copy the matching public key line for ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or download it as .pub.
- **Private**: Your key is converted in this browser tab and never sent anywhere.

### How to convert a PPK file to PEM

1. **Open the .ppk file** — Click **Open a key file** and choose your .ppk, or paste its text.
2. **Unlock it** — If the key has a passphrase, enter it and click **Unlock**.
3. **Choose the format** — Pick **PEM** (or **OpenSSH** / **PKCS#8**) and optionally a new passphrase.
4. **Download** — Click **Convert**, then **Download**. On macOS/Linux run `chmod 600` on the file before using it.

### Guide

#### PEM or OpenSSH — which do I need?

Ed25519 keys have no traditional PEM form, so choosing PEM gives the standard PKCS#8 “BEGIN PRIVATE KEY” format instead.

| Use | Choose |
| --- | --- |
| ssh on macOS/Linux, Git, VS Code Remote | OpenSSH (or PEM — both work) |
| AWS EC2 .pem files, older tools, Paramiko | PEM |
| Java, Node.js, Python cryptography libraries | PKCS#8 |
| An older PuTTY or WinSCP that rejects new keys | PPK v2 |

#### Using the converted key

Save it in `~/.ssh` (for example `~/.ssh/id_rsa`) and run `chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa` — ssh refuses keys that other users can read. Then connect with `ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa user@server`.

Need it the other way round? Use the [PEM to PPK converter](https://justtools.online/security-tools/pem-to-ppk/).

### FAQ

**How do I convert a PPK file to PEM?**
Open the .ppk file here, enter its passphrase if it has one, choose PEM and click Convert. Download the new key — no PuTTYgen needed.

**Does it work with PuTTY’s new PPK version 3 files?**
Yes. PPK v3 (PuTTY 0.75 and later), including keys protected with Argon2 passphrases, and older v2 files are both supported.

**Is it safe to convert a private key online?**
The conversion runs in your browser and the key is never uploaded, so it’s as private as converting on your own computer. Still, use only sites you trust with keys, and delete spare copies afterwards.

**What if I forgot the passphrase?**
It can’t be recovered — the passphrase is what decrypts the key. You’ll need to create a new key pair and add its public key to your servers.

**Why does ssh say “bad permissions” or “unprotected private key”?**
The key file is readable by other users. Run `chmod 600` on it (or remove other users’ access on Windows), then try again.

**Can I convert DSA keys?**
Yes, but OpenSSH 9.8 and later no longer accept DSA (ssh-dss) keys. Create a new Ed25519 key for new servers.

Convert a PEM or OpenSSH private key (id_rsa, AWS .pem) to a PuTTY .ppk file online — PPK v3 or v2, with an optional passphrase. Free, private, no upload.

### How to convert a PEM file to PPK

### Guide

#### Using the .ppk file

**PuTTY:** Connection → SSH → Auth → Credentials → “Private key file for authentication”, then save the session.

**WinSCP:** Login → Advanced → SSH → Authentication → Private key file. **FileZilla:** Settings → Connection → SFTP → Add key file.

Going the other way? Use the [PPK to PEM converter](https://justtools.online/security-tools/ppk-to-pem/).

#### PPK v3 or v2?

|  | PPK v3 | PPK v2 |
| --- | --- | --- |

### FAQ

**How do I convert a PEM file to PPK?**
Open the .pem file here, enter its passphrase if it has one, choose PPK v3 and click Convert. Then download the .ppk — no PuTTYgen needed.

**Can I convert an AWS EC2 .pem key to .ppk?**
Yes. AWS key pairs download as PEM files; convert them to .ppk here and load them in PuTTY or WinSCP. Connect as the instance’s user, such as ec2-user or ubuntu.

**Does it support new OpenSSH keys (BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY)?**
Yes, including passphrase-protected ones. Unlocking takes a second or two because OpenSSH deliberately makes passphrase checks slow.

**PuTTY says “unsupported key format” — what now?**
Your PuTTY is probably older than 0.75. Convert again choosing **PPK v2**, or update PuTTY.

**Is it safe to convert a private key online?**
The conversion happens in your browser and the key is never uploaded. Use only tools you trust with private keys, and delete spare copies afterwards.

**Which key types are supported?**
RSA, ECDSA (P-256, P-384, P-521), Ed25519 and DSA. Ed448 and security-key (sk-) keys aren’t supported by PuTTY’s format here.

- **Check before you pay**: UPI codes show the payee’s name, UPI ID and amount, with a reminder that you never scan a code to receive money.
- **Safer links**: See the real website first, with warnings for unencrypted pages, shorteners, look-alike addresses and app downloads.
- **Wi-Fi in a tap**: Read the network name and password from a Wi-Fi QR code and copy the password.
- **Many codes at once**: Keep scanning to read a stack of codes, then copy them all or export a CSV.
- **Private**: Nothing is uploaded or recorded. The camera turns off when you stop or leave the page.

### How to scan a QR code online

1. **Choose the source** — Use **Camera**, or **Image or screenshot** for a picture on your device.
2. **Scan** — Click **Start camera** and allow access, then hold the code inside the frame — or drop/paste the image.
3. **Check what it contains** — Read the link, payment or details shown, including any warnings.
4. **Use it** — Open the link, copy the text, save the contact or event — only when you choose.

### Guide

#### Staying safe with QR codes

A QR code is just text, so anyone can print one — scammers stick fake codes over real ones on parking meters, posters and shop counters. Always check the website address before entering passwords or card details, and be careful with links from shorteners or bare IP addresses.

For **UPI** payments, check that the name your UPI app shows matches who you want to pay. You never need to scan a QR code or enter your UPI PIN to **receive** money — that’s a common fraud.

#### If a code won’t scan

Move closer so the code fills most of the frame, hold steady, and add light — on phones, tap **Light** for the torch. For images, use a sharp, straight photo or a screenshot rather than a photo of a screen.

Need to make a code instead? Use the [QR Code Generator](https://justtools.online/qr-tools/qr-code-generator/). For product barcodes, use the [Barcode Scanner](https://justtools.online/qr-tools/barcode-scanner/).

Open this page, click **Start camera** and hold the code up to your webcam — or take a screenshot of the code and paste it with Ctrl+V.

**Can I scan a QR code from an image or screenshot?**
Yes. Choose **Image or screenshot**, then drop the file or paste it. Every code in the image is read.

**Is it safe to scan unknown QR codes?**
Scanning here is safe — nothing opens until you click. The scanner shows the real destination and warns about common tricks, but always check the address before entering passwords or paying.

**Why isn’t the camera working?**
Your browser may have blocked camera access for this site — allow it in the site settings — or another app may be using the camera. You can always scan a photo instead.

**Are the camera images saved or uploaded?**
No. Frames are decoded on your device and discarded immediately; nothing is recorded or sent anywhere.

**Does it read UPI and Wi-Fi QR codes?**
Yes. UPI codes show the payee, UPI ID and amount; Wi-Fi codes show the network name, security type and password.

### Guide

#### What the GS1 prefix tells you

The first digits of an EAN-13 show which national GS1 office gave the company its barcode numbers — 890 for GS1 India, 400–440 for Germany, 690–699 for China. They **don’t** prove where the product was made: a company registered in India can make goods anywhere, and vice versa.

Yes — GS1 DataMatrix codes on medicines are decoded into the product number (GTIN), batch, expiry date and serial number.

### Guide

#### What the SEO checker looks at

| Area | What is checked | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Search appearance | Title, meta description, favicon | They make up your result in Google and Bing, and decide whether people click. |
| Crawling & indexing | HTTP status, robots meta tag, robots.txt, sitemap, canonical, HTTPS, URL, hreflang | A single noindex or Disallow keeps the page out of search results entirely. |

#### How the score works

Every check has a weight by how much it affects search: the title, meta description and H1 count most, a missing X card least. A passed check earns its full weight, a warning half, a failure nothing; notes marked with an “i” are advice and don’t count. Each area gets its own score, so you can see at a glance whether the trouble is content, indexing or technical.

**If search engines can’t index the page at all** — an error status, a noindex tag or a robots.txt block — the score is capped at 30, because nothing else matters until that is fixed. A high score means the page is technically ready to rank; how well it ranks still depends on the quality of the content, links from other sites and the competition.

#### SEO for AI search (GEO)

ChatGPT search, Claude, Perplexity and Google’s AI Overviews answer questions by reading web pages and citing them. To be one of those sources, a page has to be **crawlable by their bots** (OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot, and Googlebot for AI Overviews), **quotable** (no nosnippet or tiny max-snippet), and **readable without JavaScript**, because most AI crawlers don’t run it.

Blocking training crawlers such as GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot or Google-Extended is a separate choice: it keeps your content out of model training but doesn’t remove you from search or from AI answers. The checker lists both kinds separately so you can decide. Clear headings, direct answers, FAQs and structured data help AI tools understand and quote a page; llms.txt is an optional extra that Google doesn’t use.

Keep titles to about 50–60 characters — Google cuts them at roughly 600 pixels — and meta descriptions to 120–160 characters. Bing Webmaster Tools reports descriptions shorter than about 25 or longer than 160 characters as an error.

It depends on what you want. Blocking training crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, CCBot, Google-Extended) keeps your content out of AI training without hurting search. Blocking AI search crawlers (OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot) means those assistants can’t cite or link to you.

2. **Read the results** — See the **network address**, **broadcast address**, usable host range and number of hosts instantly.

4. **Export** — Copy the details or download the subnet table as CSV for your documentation.

### Guide

#### IPv4 subnet mask cheat sheet

| Prefix | Subnet mask | Wildcard | Addresses | Usable hosts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| /8 | 255.0.0.0 | 0.255.255.255 | 16,777,216 | 16,777,214 |
| /16 | 255.255.0.0 | 0.0.255.255 | 65,536 | 65,534 |
| /20 | 255.255.240.0 | 0.0.15.255 | 4,096 | 4,094 |
| /21 | 255.255.248.0 | 0.0.7.255 | 2,048 | 2,046 |
| /22 | 255.255.252.0 | 0.0.3.255 | 1,024 | 1,022 |
| /23 | 255.255.254.0 | 0.0.1.255 | 512 | 510 |
| /24 | 255.255.255.0 | 0.0.0.255 | 256 | 254 |
| /25 | 255.255.255.128 | 0.0.0.127 | 128 | 126 |
| /26 | 255.255.255.192 | 0.0.0.63 | 64 | 62 |
| /27 | 255.255.255.224 | 0.0.0.31 | 32 | 30 |
| /28 | 255.255.255.240 | 0.0.0.15 | 16 | 14 |
| /29 | 255.255.255.248 | 0.0.0.7 | 8 | 6 |
| /30 | 255.255.255.252 | 0.0.0.3 | 4 | 2 |
| /31 | 255.255.255.254 | 0.0.0.1 | 2 | 2 (point-to-point) |
| /32 | 255.255.255.255 | 0.0.0.0 | 1 | 1 (single host) |

#### Private and special IPv4 ranges

| Range | Use |
| --- | --- |
| 10.0.0.0/8 | Private network (RFC 1918) — large companies and data centres |
| 172.16.0.0/12 | Private network (RFC 1918) — 172.16.0.0 to 172.31.255.255 |
| 192.168.0.0/16 | Private network (RFC 1918) — home and office routers |
| 100.64.0.0/10 | Carrier-grade NAT — ISPs, especially mobile data, share public IPs |
| 169.254.0.0/16 | Link-local — self-assigned when DHCP fails |
| 127.0.0.0/8 | Loopback — the computer itself (localhost) |

#### How subnetting works

An IPv4 address has 32 bits. The prefix length — the number after the slash — says how many of them identify the network; the rest number the hosts inside it. A /24 leaves 8 host bits, so 2⁸ = 256 addresses. The first is the **network address** and the last the **broadcast address**, so 254 are usable for devices.

Every extra prefix bit halves the block: a /24 splits into two /25s, four /26s or eight /27s. **VLSM** (variable-length subnet masking) uses different sizes inside one network — a /25 for 100 office PCs, a /30 for a router link — to avoid wasting addresses. IPv6 LANs simply use /64 each; sites usually get a /48 or /56.

### FAQ

**How many usable hosts does a /24 have?**
254. A /24 has 256 addresses, but the first (network) and last (broadcast) can’t be given to devices. In general, usable hosts = 2^(32 − prefix) − 2, except /31 and /32.

**What is a wildcard mask?**
The inverse of the subnet mask: 0 bits must match and 1 bits can be anything. For 255.255.255.0 it is 0.0.0.255. Cisco access lists and OSPF network statements use wildcard masks.

**How do I find the network and broadcast address?**
The network address is the IP with all host bits set to 0 (a bitwise AND with the mask); the broadcast address has all host bits set to 1. For 192.168.1.10/24 they are 192.168.1.0 and 192.168.1.255.

**Can a /31 be used?**
Yes, on point-to-point links between two routers. RFC 3021 lets both addresses be used because a link with two ends needs no broadcast address.

**What subnet size should I use for an IPv6 LAN?**
A /64. Stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) needs it, and a /64 still holds 18 quintillion addresses. Give each site a /48 or /56 to split into /64s.

**What is VLSM?**
Variable-length subnet masking: dividing one network into subnets of different sizes to match each LAN’s needs. Allocate the largest subnet first so every block stays aligned — the VLSM tab does this for you.

## Internet Speed Test

URL: https://justtools.online/network-tools/internet-speed-test/
Category: Internet & Network Tools
Processing: Contacts an external service to work (see the page).
Last updated: 2026-10-06

Free internet speed test: check download and upload speed, ping, jitter and bufferbloat on Wi-Fi, broadband or mobile data — no app, with a data saver mode.

### At a glance

- Measures **download and upload speed** in Mbps, **ping** (latency) and **jitter**, plus **loaded latency** — how much ping rises while the line is busy (bufferbloat).
- Tests against **Cloudflare’s global network** (speed.cloudflare.com), usually from a data centre in or near your city; the page shows which one.
- Leaves out connection set-up and server processing time, and reports the 90th-percentile speed of many transfers — the line’s real capacity rather than its slow start.
- File sizes grow only while transfers stay quick, and **Data saver** caps a run at about 39 MB for mobile data.
- Rates the connection for 4K streaming, video calls, online gaming, browsing and uploads, and shows which data centre answered, your country and your IP address.
- Keeps your last 20 results in this browser only. No app or account is needed, and JustTools never sees your results.

### Features

- **All the numbers that matter**: Download, upload, ping, jitter and loaded latency — not just one big number.
- **Live gauge**: Watch the speed as it is measured, from a quick ping to the full download and upload runs.
- **Bufferbloat grade**: See whether calls and games will lag while someone else downloads, graded A+ to F.
- **Mobile-data friendly**: Data saver mode keeps a test under about 39 MB, and you can stop at any moment.
- **What it’s good for**: Plain ratings for streaming, video calls, gaming, browsing and uploading files.
- **Your history**: Compare Wi-Fi with cable, or morning with evening — recent results stay in your browser.

### How to test your internet speed

1. **Close heavy apps** — Pause downloads, streaming and cloud backups on all devices so they don’t share the line during the test.
2. **Press Start** — Choose **Full test**, or **Data saver** on mobile data, and press **Start**. Ping is measured first.
3. **Wait for both runs** — Download and then upload are measured, which takes 15–30 seconds on most connections.
4. **Read the results** — Compare download and upload with your plan, check the ratings, and copy the results to share with your provider.

### Guide

#### What the results mean

| Result | What it measures | Good value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Download | How fast data reaches you — streaming, browsing, downloads | 25 Mbps+ for 4K; 100 Mbps+ for busy homes |
| Upload | How fast you send data — video calls, uploads, cloud backup | 5 Mbps+ for HD calls; 20 Mbps+ for creators |
| Ping | Round-trip time to the server, in milliseconds | Under 30 ms great, under 100 ms fine |
| Jitter | How much ping varies from one moment to the next | Under 10 ms for gaming, under 30 ms for calls |
| Loaded latency | Ping while the line is busy downloading or uploading | Within 30 ms of the idle ping (grade A) |

#### Why your speed may be lower than your plan

- **Wi-Fi**: walls, distance and older routers or phones cut speed. Test with a cable, or close to the router on 5 GHz, to see what the line delivers.
- **Other devices**: TVs, updates and backups on the same connection share the bandwidth during the test.
- **Peak hours**: evenings are busiest, especially on mobile networks and shared fibre.
- **VPNs and proxies** add distance and encryption overhead.
- **Very fast plans**: above roughly 1 Gbps, the browser and device can become the limit rather than the line.

### FAQ

**How accurate is this speed test?**
It uses the same method as Cloudflare’s own test: precise browser timings, server time removed, and the 90th-percentile speed of many transfers. Results from different test sites differ a little because they use different servers and methods.

**How much data does a speed test use?**
It depends on your speed: a full test uses up to a few hundred MB on a very fast line, less on slower ones. Data saver mode uses at most about 39 MB — the page shows the exact amount after each test.

**What is a good ping for gaming?**
Under 30 ms is excellent and under 60 ms is good for most online games; jitter should stay below about 10–20 ms. Above 100 ms you will notice lag in fast-paced games.

**What is the difference between Mbps and MB/s?**
Speeds are quoted in megabits per second (Mbps); file sizes in megabytes. One byte is 8 bits, so 100 Mbps downloads about 12.5 MB per second.

**Is the speed test private?**
The test connects your browser to Cloudflare’s speed test servers, which see your IP address like any website does. JustTools doesn’t receive or store your results; your history stays in your browser.

**Why is upload slower than download?**
Most home and mobile plans are asymmetric — designed to receive more than they send. Fibre plans are often symmetric, so similar upload and download speeds are normal there.

## JWT Debugger

URL: https://justtools.online/developer-tools/jwt-debugger/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-06

Decode any JWT and verify its signature in your browser: header, claims and expiry explained; HS256, RS256, ES256 and EdDSA with PEM or JWK keys. No upload.

### At a glance

- Decodes the **header and payload** of any JWT, explains standard and common claims (iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, scope, roles …) and shows times in UTC and your local time.
- Shows whether the token is **expired, not yet valid or still valid**, with a live countdown.
- **Verifies the signature** for HS256/384/512, RS256/384/512, PS256/384/512, ES256/384/512 and EdDSA (Ed25519) using your browser’s Web Crypto.
- Accepts keys as a shared secret (text, Base64, Base64URL or hex), **PEM** public or private keys, PKCS#1, X.509 certificates, a **JWK** or a whole **JWKS**, picking the key by kid.
- Warns about real security problems: alg “none”, keys or key URLs supplied by the token itself (jwk, jku, x5u), missing expiry, weak or well-known secrets and secrets placed in the payload.
- Runs entirely in your browser — tokens and keys are never uploaded or logged — and also decodes the header of encrypted JWE tokens.

### Features

- **Claims in plain English**: Every claim labelled — issuer, audience, scopes, roles — with dates converted and the time left until expiry.
- **Real signature check**: Verifies with Web Crypto, the same cryptography your browser uses for HTTPS, for every common JWS algorithm.
- **Any key format**: Secrets, PEM, PKCS#1, certificates, JWK or a JWKS from your identity provider — no conversion needed.
- **Security warnings**: Flags unsigned tokens, embedded keys, long lifetimes and weak secrets before they cause trouble.
- **Private by design**: Nothing leaves your device, so production tokens are safe to inspect.
- **Build tokens too**: Switch to Encode & sign to create a test token, then verify it here in one click.

### How to decode and verify a JWT

1. **Paste the token** — Paste the JWT — a “Bearer …” header value works too. The header, payload and claims appear instantly.
2. **Check the claims** — Read who issued the token, who it’s for and when it **expires**; warnings appear above the claims.
3. **Add the key** — Enter the **secret** for HS256, or paste the **public key**, certificate or JWKS for RS256, ES256 and EdDSA.
4. **Read the result** — “Signature verified” means the token is authentic and unchanged; otherwise check the key or the token.

### Guide

#### Anatomy of a JWT

| Part | Contains | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Header | The signing algorithm and token type, Base64URL-encoded JSON | {"alg":"RS256","typ":"JWT","kid":"key-1"} |
| Payload | The claims: who the token is about, for whom, and how long it lasts | {"sub":"42","aud":"api","exp":1767229200} |
| Signature | Proof that header and payload came from the key holder unchanged | Base64URL bytes of an HMAC, RSA, ECDSA or EdDSA signature |

#### Decoding is not verifying

Anyone can decode a JWT — the header and payload are only Base64URL-encoded, not encrypted. That is why tokens must never carry passwords or other secrets. **Verifying** checks the signature with the right key, which proves who created the token and that nobody changed a single character.

A server should verify the signature, then check **exp**, **nbf**, **iss** and **aud**, and accept only the algorithms it expects. Never trust the alg value or a key that arrives inside the token itself. Public keys for providers such as Auth0, Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Cognito and Firebase are published at a JWKS URL, usually ending in /.well-known/jwks.json.

### FAQ

**Is it safe to paste a production token here?**
Yes — decoding and verification run in your browser and nothing is sent to a server. Still, treat tokens like passwords: anyone holding a valid token can use it until it expires.

**Why does it say “Invalid signature”?**
The key doesn’t match the token, or the token was changed. Common causes: the wrong environment’s secret, a secret stored as Base64 but entered as text (switch the encoding), or a JWKS key with a different kid.

**Where do I find the public key to verify RS256 tokens?**
Identity providers publish them as a JWK set, usually at https://your-issuer/.well-known/jwks.json (OpenID Connect discovery lists the exact URL). Paste the whole JWKS — the key matching the token’s kid is used.

**Can it decrypt JWE tokens?**
No. Encrypted tokens (five parts) can only be read with the recipient’s private key; the debugger shows their header and says so.

**Why are exp and iat such large numbers?**
JWT times are seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC (Unix time). The debugger converts them to dates. Values in milliseconds are a common bug and are flagged.

## JWT Encoder

URL: https://justtools.online/developer-tools/jwt-encoder/
Category: Developer Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-06

Create and sign JWTs in your browser with HS256, RS256, PS256, ES256 or EdDSA: edit claims, set expiry, generate keys and a JWKS. Keys never leave your device.

### At a glance

- Signs JWTs with **HS256/384/512, RS256/384/512, PS256/384/512, ES256/384/512 and EdDSA (Ed25519)** using your browser’s Web Crypto API.
- Edits the header and payload as JSON, pointing to the line and column of any mistake; **alg** is kept in step with the algorithm you pick.
- Adds **iat, exp** (15 minutes to 30 days), **nbf** and a random **jti** in one click.
- Generates a **secure random secret** of the right length, or an RSA, EC or Ed25519 **key pair** with the public key as PEM, JWK and JWKS (kid = RFC 7638 thumbprint).
- Signs with keys in PEM (PKCS#8, PKCS#1 or SEC1) or JWK form, and warns when an HMAC secret is too short or a well-known example.
- One click opens the new token in the JWT Debugger to verify it. Everything runs locally; keys never leave your device.

### Features

- **Every JWS algorithm**: HMAC, RSA, RSA-PSS, ECDSA and EdDSA — tokens your backend libraries accept.
- **Claim shortcuts**: Issued-at, expiry, not-before and a unique ID added with one click, in seconds since 1970 as the standard requires.
- **Key generator**: Fresh 2048-bit RSA, P-256/384/521 or Ed25519 key pairs, with the public JWK and JWKS ready for your config.
- **Strong secrets**: Random HMAC secrets of the full hash length, so tokens can’t be cracked offline.
- **Verify instantly**: Send the token and key to the debugger to check the signature and claims.
- **Local only**: No server signs anything — safe for test keys, and nothing is logged.

### How to create a JWT

1. **Pick the algorithm** — Choose **HS256** for a shared secret, or **RS256**, **ES256** or **EdDSA** for a key pair.
2. **Write the claims** — Edit the payload JSON and use the buttons to add **iat** and an **exp** such as 1 hour.
3. **Add a key** — Paste your secret or private key, or click **Generate** for a new one.
4. **Copy the token** — The signed token updates as you type. Copy it, or open it in the debugger to verify.

### Guide

#### Which algorithm should I use?

| Algorithm | Key | Use it when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HS256 | One shared secret (32+ random bytes) | The same service creates and checks the tokens |
| RS256 | RSA key pair (2048-bit or more) | Others verify with your public key — the most widely supported choice |
| PS256 | RSA key pair | You want RSA with the more modern PSS padding |
| ES256 | EC P-256 key pair | Small, fast signatures with public-key verification |
| EdDSA | Ed25519 key pair | Modern, fast and hard to misuse, where your libraries support it |

#### Good practice for tokens

- Keep access tokens short-lived — minutes to an hour — and use refresh tokens for longer sessions.
- Always set **iss**, **aud** and **exp**, and have servers check them along with the signature.
- Put only what the receiver needs in the payload: it is readable by anyone who holds the token.
- Use a random secret at least as long as the hash (32 bytes for HS256) and never commit it to source control.

### FAQ

**Is it safe to sign tokens with my real keys here?**
Signing happens entirely in your browser and nothing is sent or stored. For production keys, the safest habit is still to sign on your own servers; this tool is ideal for test and development tokens.

**How long should a JWT secret be?**
At least as long as the hash: 32 random bytes for HS256, 48 for HS384 and 64 for HS512 (RFC 7518). “Generate secret” creates one of the right length.

**What format should the private key be in?**
PEM is easiest: “BEGIN PRIVATE KEY” (PKCS#8), “BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY” or “BEGIN EC PRIVATE KEY” all work, as does a private JWK. Passphrase-protected keys must be decrypted first.

**Why is exp a number like 1767229200?**
JWT dates are seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. The expiry buttons calculate it for you from the current time.

**Can I create a token without a signature?**
No. Unsigned tokens (alg “none”) can be forged by anyone, and secure libraries reject them, so this tool always signs.

## Sitemap Generator

URL: https://justtools.online/seo-tools/sitemap-generator/
Category: SEO & Marketing Tools
Processing: Contacts an external service to work (see the page).
Last updated: 2026-10-06

Free XML sitemap generator: crawl your site or paste URLs, skip noindex, redirected and robots.txt-blocked pages, add lastmod and images, ready for Google.

### At a glance

- **Crawls** a website from its home page, following links on the same host — up to 1,000 pages — or builds a sitemap from a **pasted list**, a CSV or an existing sitemap.
- Includes only **indexable pages**: it obeys robots.txt, and leaves out pages with noindex, a canonical pointing elsewhere, redirects and error statuses — listing each one with the reason.
- Adds **lastmod** from the page’s own date (article:modified_time, JSON-LD dateModified) or the server’s Last-Modified header, or a date you choose.
- Optionally adds **images** (Google image sitemap extension) and linked PDF files; changefreq and priority are optional because Google ignores them.
- Splits large sites into several files with a **sitemap index** at the protocol’s 50,000-URL / 50 MB limit, and also exports a plain-text list.
- Pages are fetched by your browser when the site allows it, otherwise through Jina Reader at about 18 pages a minute. Only page addresses are sent.

### Features

- **Crawls like Google**: Follows links, respects robots.txt and nofollow, and only keeps pages that can actually be indexed.
- **Clean by default**: No duplicates, no redirects, no noindex pages and no tracking parameters — the mistakes Search Console reports.
- **Honest lastmod**: Dates come from the pages themselves, so Google can trust them to spot updates.
- **Image sitemaps**: Add each page’s images to help them appear in Google Images.
- **Any size**: Sitemap index and numbered files are made automatically for very large sites.
- **From a list too**: Paste URLs or open a CSV or old sitemap to clean it up and rebuild it.

### How to create an XML sitemap

1. **Enter your website** — Type your home page address and choose how many pages to crawl, or switch to **From a list of URLs**.
2. **Let it crawl** — Pages are discovered through links; skipped pages are listed with the reason. You can stop at any time.
3. **Choose the details** — Pick where **lastmod** comes from and whether to add images; leave changefreq and priority out unless you need them.
4. **Upload and submit** — Download **sitemap.xml**, upload it to your site’s root, add it to robots.txt and submit it in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.

### Guide

#### What belongs in a sitemap

| Include | Leave out |
| --- | --- |
| Pages that return 200 and that you want in search results | Pages with noindex, or blocked in robots.txt |
| The canonical version of each page | Duplicates, ?ref= and other tracking variants |
| The final address after redirects | URLs that redirect or return 404 |
| Accurate lastmod dates | Dates that change on every build without a real update |

#### Do I need a sitemap?

Search engines find most pages by following links, but a sitemap helps them discover new and updated pages faster — especially on new sites with few backlinks, large sites, and pages that few other pages link to. Google reads **loc** and an accurate **lastmod**; it ignores changefreq and priority.

After uploading, list the sitemap in robots.txt (Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml) so every search engine finds it, and submit it once in Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools to see how many pages are indexed. Google no longer accepts sitemap “pings”; Bing and Yandex also support IndexNow for instant updates.

### FAQ

**Is the sitemap generator free?**
Yes, with no sign-up. Crawls are limited to 1,000 pages at a time; for bigger sites, crawl sections separately or use the URL list mode with an export from your CMS.

**Why is the crawl slow for my site?**
If your site doesn’t allow other websites to read its pages (most don’t), pages are fetched through Jina Reader, whose free service allows about 20 requests a minute — so 100 pages take around 6 minutes. Sites that allow it are crawled several pages at a time.

**Why were some pages left out?**
They can’t be indexed as they are: blocked by robots.txt, marked noindex, redirected, returning an error, or pointing to a different canonical URL. The “Pages left out” list shows the reason for each.

**Should I set changefreq and priority?**
Not for Google — it ignores both. They are optional and left out by default; an accurate lastmod is far more useful.

**How many URLs can one sitemap hold?**
50,000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed. Larger sites need several sitemap files listed in a sitemap index, which the generator creates automatically.

## Robots.txt Generator

URL: https://justtools.online/seo-tools/robots-txt-generator/
Category: SEO & Marketing Tools
Processing: Contacts an external service to work (see the page).
Last updated: 2026-10-06

Create a robots.txt file free: block admin pages, AI training bots like GPTBot or SEO crawlers, add your sitemap, then test any URL against Google’s rules.

### At a glance

- Generates robots.txt from simple choices: default access, paths to block with exceptions, an optional Crawl-delay and your **sitemap** URLs.
- Lets you allow or block **26 named crawlers** in four groups — search engines, AI search assistants (OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot, PerplexityBot), **AI training bots** (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, CCBot …) and SEO crawlers (AhrefsBot, SemrushBot …).
- Presets for WordPress, online shops, staging sites, and blocking AI training while staying in search and AI answers.
- **Validates** any robots.txt with line numbers: rules outside a group, unsupported noindex, misspellings, relative sitemaps, blocked CSS and JavaScript, and Google’s 500 KiB limit.
- **Tests a URL** against every crawler using Google’s matching rules (RFC 9309): the most specific user-agent group, the longest matching path, Allow winning ties — and shows the line that decided.
- Loads a site’s live robots.txt for checking — directly from your browser when the site allows it, otherwise through Jina Reader. Building and testing happen on your device.

### Features

- **Correct by construction**: Groups, paths and sitemap lines are written the way Google, Bing and AI crawlers expect, with full sitemap URLs.
- **AI crawler control**: Opt out of AI training without disappearing from ChatGPT, Claude or Perplexity search answers — or block AI completely.
- **Smart presets**: WordPress, online shop, staging and AI presets give a sensible starting point in one click.
- **Validator with line numbers**: Finds the mistakes that silently break robots.txt — and jumps to the line.
- **URL tester**: See which crawlers may fetch a page and which rule decides, before you upload the file.
- **Check any live site**: Load a website’s robots.txt to audit it, or to start editing your own.

### How to create a robots.txt file

1. **Pick a starting point** — Choose a preset such as **WordPress** or **Block AI training**, or start from **Allow everything**.
2. **Add your rules** — List paths to keep out of search (like /admin/), allow or block specific crawlers, and add your sitemap URL.
3. **Test it** — Click **Test a URL against this file** to check important pages are still crawlable.
4. **Upload** — Download robots.txt and upload it to your site’s root so it opens at example.com/robots.txt.

### Guide

#### robots.txt rules at a glance

| Line | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User-agent | Which crawler the following rules are for; * means all | User-agent: GPTBot |
| Disallow | Paths the crawler must not fetch | Disallow: /admin/ |
| Allow | An exception inside a disallowed path | Allow: /admin/help/ |
| * | Matches any characters | Disallow: /*?sort= |
| $ | Marks the end of the URL | Disallow: /*.pdf$ |
| Sitemap | Full URL of a sitemap, anywhere in the file | Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml |

#### What robots.txt can and can’t do

robots.txt controls **crawling**, not indexing. A blocked page can still appear in Google as a bare link if other sites link to it, and Google can’t see a noindex tag on a page it isn’t allowed to fetch. To keep a page out of search results, allow crawling and add **<meta name="robots" content="noindex">** instead.

It is also public and voluntary: well-behaved crawlers such as Googlebot, Bingbot, GPTBot and ClaudeBot obey it, but it is not access control. Never list secret paths in it, and protect private areas with a login.

### FAQ

**Where do I put robots.txt?**
In the root of your domain, so it opens at https://example.com/robots.txt. Each subdomain (blog.example.com) needs its own file, and it must be plain text returning HTTP 200.

**How do I block ChatGPT and other AI bots?**
Add a group for each crawler with Disallow: /. To stop training only, block GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, CCBot and similar; to also leave AI search answers, block OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot and PerplexityBot. The “Block AI training” and “Block all AI” presets do this for you.

**Will blocking Google-Extended remove my site from Google Search?**
No. Google-Extended only controls whether Gemini may use your content for training and grounding. Search, including AI Overviews, uses Googlebot.

**Does Google follow Crawl-delay?**
No. Bing and Yandex do; Google adjusts its crawl rate automatically. If Googlebot overloads your server, return 503 or 429 temporarily.

**Why does the validator say noindex isn’t supported?**
Google stopped honouring Noindex lines in robots.txt in September 2019. Use a robots meta tag or the X-Robots-Tag HTTP header on the page instead.

**Is blocking CSS and JavaScript a problem?**
Yes. Google renders pages like a browser; without your CSS and JavaScript it may see a broken page and rank it lower. Keep folders such as /wp-includes/ and /_next/ crawlable.

## Tic Tac Toe

URL: https://justtools.online/games/tic-tac-toe/
Category: Games
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-07

Play Tic Tac Toe online free against the computer — Easy, Medium or unbeatable Hard — or with a friend on one device. 3×3 to 6×6 boards. No sign-up.

### At a glance

- Play against the computer on **Easy**, **Medium** or **Hard**, or with a friend taking turns on the same phone, tablet or computer.
- On the classic 3×3 board, Hard plays perfectly and **never loses** — the best anyone can do against it is a draw.
- Bigger boards for a longer game: **4×4, 5×5 and 6×6**, with 3, 4 or 5 in a row to win.
- Classic Tic Tac Toe has **255,168 possible games**: X wins 131,184, O wins 77,904 and 46,080 end in a draw. With perfect play it is always a draw.
- Hints, undo, sound, full screen and keyboard play; scores are kept for each mode and board on your device. Free, with no download or sign-up.

### Features

- **Three difficulty levels**: Easy for young children, Medium for a fair fight, and a Hard opponent that never loses on 3×3.
- **Two players, one device**: Pass and play with a friend, with your own names and a running score.
- **Bigger boards**: Try 4×4, 5×5 or 6×6 with 3, 4 or 5 in a row — the computer thinks several moves ahead.
- **Learn as you play**: Ask for a hint to see the best move, or take a move back and try another idea.
- **Fair starts**: The first move swaps sides every round, so nobody always has the advantage.
- **Plays anywhere**: Works on phones, tablets and computers, with keyboard controls and screen reader announcements.

### How to play Tic Tac Toe

1. **Choose an opponent** — Pick **Computer** and a difficulty, and whether you play X or O — or pick **A friend** to play on the same device.
2. **Choose a board** — Keep the classic 3×3 board, or try 4×4, 5×5 or 6×6 and choose how many in a row it takes to win.
3. **Take turns** — Tap an empty square to place your mark. The first to complete a line across, down or diagonally wins; a full board with no line is a draw.
4. **Play again** — Press **Play again** for the next round — the score keeps adding up. Use **Hint** or **Undo** while you learn.

### Guide

#### The rules

Two players take turns placing their mark — X or O — in an empty square of a 3×3 grid. The first player to get three of their marks in a row, column or diagonal wins. If all nine squares fill up with no line, the game is a draw.

The game is also called **noughts and crosses** in Britain and **zero kata** in India. On bigger boards the idea is the same, but you need the number in a row shown under the board.

#### How to never lose at 3×3

- No first move wins by force: with best play from both sides, every opening ends in a draw.
- If your opponent starts in a **corner**, take the **centre** — every other reply loses against perfect play.
- If they start in the **centre**, take a **corner**. Answering on an edge loses.
- If they start on an **edge**, take the centre, a corner next to their mark, or the edge opposite it.
- On every turn, first look for a winning move, then block any two-in-a-row of theirs.
- Win with a **fork**: a move that makes two lines of two at once, so your opponent can only block one.

#### Tic Tac Toe by the numbers

| Classic 3×3 | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Possible games (until someone wins or the board fills) | 255,168 |
| … won by X (who moves first) | 131,184 |
| … won by O | 77,904 |
| … drawn | 46,080 |
| Positions that can occur in a game | 5,478 |
| Different positions, counting rotations and mirror images once | 765 |
| Result with perfect play | Draw |

### FAQ

**Can you beat the computer on Hard?**
Not on the 3×3 board: Hard plays perfectly, so the best possible result is a draw. On bigger boards it looks several moves ahead in about a second per move, so strong players can still win.

**How do I play with a friend?**
Choose **A friend** under Play against, add your names if you like, and take turns on the same phone or computer. Playing over the internet on two devices isn’t available.

**Who goes first?**
X moves first in a normal game. With **Take turns going first** switched on (the default), the first move swaps between the players every round, which keeps things fair.

**Is Tic Tac Toe always a draw?**
With perfect play by both players, yes — the classic 3×3 game always ends in a draw. Games are won when someone misses a block or falls for a fork.

**Is it free, and does it need the internet?**
It’s free with no download or sign-up. Once the page has loaded, the game runs entirely in your browser, so it keeps working if your connection drops.

**Are my scores saved?**
Yes, in this browser only, with a separate score for each mode, difficulty and board size. **Reset score** clears the one you are playing.

Pick colours from any image: get HEX, RGB, HSL and CMYK codes with a zoom loupe, plus the image’s colour palette. Free, private — nothing is uploaded.
