### Guide

#### How Markdown maps to Notion blocks

| Markdown | Notion block | API type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `# Heading` to `#### Heading` | Heading 1 to 4 | `heading_1` … `heading_4` |
| `- item`, `1. item` | Bulleted or numbered list | `bulleted_list_item`, `numbered_list_item` |
| `- [ ] task`, `- [x] done` | To-do | `to_do` |
| `> quote` | Quote | `quote` |
| `> [!NOTE]` and other GitHub alerts | Callout | `callout` |
| `<details><summary>…</summary>` | Toggle | `toggle` |
| Fenced code with a language | Code | `code` |
| `$$ … $$` | Equation | `equation` |
| A table | Table | `table` with `table_row` children |
| `---` | Divider | `divider` |
| `![alt](https://…)` | Image | `image` (external) |
| `**bold**`, `*italic*`, `~~strike~~`, `` `code` ``, `[link](url)`, `$x$` | Text styles | rich text annotations, links and inline equations |

#### Which output to use

- **Copy for Notion** — for pasting by hand. It puts ordinary formatted text on the clipboard, as copying from a web page does. Notion-only blocks have no clipboard form, so a callout is pasted as a quote and an equation as code; the API outputs create the exact block.
- **API blocks (JSON)** — for code, Zapier, Make, n8n or any tool that calls the block endpoints. Use the *Append* body with `PATCH /v1/blocks/{id}/children`, or the *New page* body with `POST /v1/pages`.
- **Notion Markdown** — for the API’s newer `markdown` parameter. It is Notion’s “enhanced markdown”: tabs for nesting, `<callout>`, `<details>` and `<table>` tags, and Notion’s escaping rules. One request can create up to 5,000 blocks.

#### The limits it works within

| Limit in Notion’s API | What the tool does |
| --- | --- |
| 2,000 characters in one piece of text | Cuts longer text into pieces inside the same block |
| 100 items in any array | Continues a longer block in the next one; splits tables over 100 rows and repeats the heading row |
| 100 blocks per request | Writes several requests, to be sent in order |
| Two levels of nesting per request | Moves deeper blocks up a level and says how many |
| 1,000 blocks and 500 KB per request | Starts a new request before either is reached |
| 1,000 characters in an equation | Keeps a longer one as LaTeX code |

#### Good to know

- Notion only links to full web addresses. Fill in **Base address for relative links** to turn `./page.md` and `images/a.png` into complete URLs.
- Images must already be online at a public https:// address; the API reference lists .png, .jpg, .gif, .svg, .bmp, .heic and .tif for external images. Upload local images in Notion itself.
- Front matter at the top of a file is left out; its `title` becomes the page title for a new page. Otherwise the first `#` heading does.
- A line break inside a paragraph is a space, as in any Markdown renderer. End a line with two spaces or `<br>` for a real line break.
- Sending is optional. If you use it, your browser sends the blocks and your token straight to api.notion.com; this site has no server that could see them, and the token is forgotten when you close the page.

### FAQ

**How do I paste Markdown into Notion so it keeps its formatting?**
Paste the Markdown here, click **Copy for Notion** and paste into your page with Ctrl+V. The clipboard then holds the headings, lists, to-dos, tables, quotes and code as formatted text, the same as when you copy them from a web page. For callouts, toggles and equations exactly as written, send the page through the API instead.

**What is the “API blocks (JSON)” output for?**
Notion’s API builds pages from block objects. This output is that JSON — the `children` array — ready to send to `PATCH /v1/blocks/{page_id}/children` or `POST /v1/pages`, or to paste into the HTTP step of an automation tool.

**Why did my content come out as several requests?**
Notion accepts at most 100 blocks in one request. Longer documents are split into parts; send them in order, each to the same page. Use the arrows above the result to move between parts.

**What happens to lists nested many levels deep?**
One request can carry two levels of children. Blocks nested deeper are moved up to the second level, in the same order, and the note below the result says how many. The Notion Markdown output has no such limit.

**Can it send the page to Notion for me?**
Yes. Open **Send it to Notion from here**, paste a Notion token and choose a new page or an existing one. Your browser calls Notion’s API directly; the token is not saved anywhere. If you would rather not paste a token into a web page, copy the JSON and send it yourself.

**Does it work with ChatGPT or Claude output?**
Yes — that is a common use. Copy the answer as Markdown and paste it here. Tables, nested lists, code and maths written as `\( … \)` or `\[ … \]` are converted to Notion tables, lists, code blocks and equations.

**Which Notion API version does the JSON follow?**
Version 2026-03-11, the current one when this tool was written, which added a fourth heading level. If your tool only knows three, set **Heading levels** to *Up to 3* under Options.

**Where do I get a Notion token?**
In Notion’s developer portal, under Personal access tokens: create a token with the Notion API capability and copy it. With such a token, leaving the parent page blank creates a private page in your workspace. A token from an internal connection also works, after you add that connection to the page under ••• → Connections.

**Is my text uploaded?**
Not unless you press Send. The conversion runs in your browser, and this site has no server that receives your text. When you do send, the blocks go from your browser to Notion and nowhere else.

## Dofollow Nofollow Link Checker

URL: https://justtools.online/seo-tools/dofollow-nofollow-checker/
Category: SEO & Marketing Tools
Processing: Contacts an external service to work (see the page).
Last updated: 2026-10-14

See which links on a page are dofollow or nofollow. Lists every link with its rel, anchor text and type, counts sponsored and UGC, and checks a backlink.

### At a glance

- Lists **every link on a page** and labels each as followed (dofollow), **nofollow**, **sponsored** or **UGC**, with its anchor text, address and rel values.
- Counts followed and nofollow links, internal and external links, different addresses and the outside sites linked to.
- Checks a **backlink**: type your domain to see each link the page gives you and whether it is followed.
- Reads the page’s robots meta tag: `<meta name="robots" content="nofollow">` makes every link on the page nofollow, and the tool counts them so.
- Treats `sponsored` and `ugc` like `nofollow`, as Google does — links with any of the three “will generally not be followed”.
- Warns about nofollow on your own internal links, links with no anchor text, and the meaningless `rel="dofollow"`.
- Works from a page address or from **pasted HTML** — useful for pages behind a login. Pasted HTML never leaves your device.
- Filter, search, copy the addresses or download the list as CSV.

### Features

- **Every link, one table**: Anchor text, full address, rel values, internal or external, the part of the page it sits in and whether it opens a new tab.
- **Backlink check in one step**: Paid for a guest post or earned a mention? Enter the page and your domain to confirm the link is there and is followed.
- **Page-wide rules included**: A robots meta tag can make a whole page nofollow without touching any link. The tool reads it, which a look at single links misses.
- **JavaScript pages too**: Turn on **Run JavaScript first** for sites that build their links in the browser, such as React or Vue apps.
- **Export**: Copy the addresses of the links you have filtered, or download them as a CSV file for a spreadsheet.
- **Careful with your data**: Only the page address is sent out to fetch the page. HTML you paste is read in your browser and goes nowhere.

### How to check dofollow and nofollow links

1. **Enter the page** — Type or paste the address of the page whose links you want to see, and click **Check links**.
2. **Read the summary** — The tiles show how many links are followed and nofollow, and how many go to other sites.
3. **Check a backlink** — Type your own domain under **Does this page link to your site?** to see the links to it and their type.
4. **Filter the list** — Show only nofollow links, only external ones, or search for a word or address.
5. **Export** — Click **Copy addresses** or **CSV** to take the filtered list with you.

### Guide

#### What the rel values mean

| In the link | Shown as | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| no rel, or only `noopener`, `noreferrer`, `external` | Followed | An ordinary link. Search engines may follow it and count it as a vote for the page it points to. |
| `rel="nofollow"` | Nofollow | The site does not want to be associated with the linked page, or have it crawled from here. |
| `rel="sponsored"` | Sponsored | An advertisement or paid placement. Google’s preferred value for paid links. |
| `rel="ugc"` | UGC | User-generated content, such as comments and forum posts. |
| `rel="ugc nofollow"` | Nofollow + UGC | Values can be combined, separated by spaces or commas. |
| `<meta name="robots" content="nofollow">` in the page | Nofollow (page) | Every link on the page is nofollow, whatever its own rel. |

#### There is no “dofollow” attribute

“Dofollow” is only a name for a normal link — one without `nofollow`, `sponsored` or `ugc`. Links are followed by default, so nothing needs to be added. Writing `rel="dofollow"` does nothing; if a page uses it, the tool says so.

Since 2019 Google has treated `nofollow`, `sponsored` and `ugc` as hints rather than strict orders: such links will generally not be followed, but Google may choose to use them. Other search engines make their own choices.

#### What counts as a link here

- Links to web pages — `<a href>` and image-map `<area href>` — are counted and labelled.
- Jumps within the same page (`#section`), e-mail and phone links and `javascript:` links do not lead to another page. They are listed under **Not pages** and left out of the counts.
- A link to the same site with or without `www.` is internal. Links to other subdomains, such as blog.example.com from example.com, count as external.
- Links inside `<noscript>` and `<template>` are ignored, as they are not part of the page a visitor sees.

#### What it cannot see

- Links added by JavaScript after the page loads, unless **Run JavaScript first** is on.
- A nofollow sent as an `X-Robots-Tag` HTTP header. Browsers do not let one website read another’s headers.
- Pages behind a login, or sites that block automated visitors. Open the page yourself, copy its source (Ctrl+U) and use **Paste HTML**.
- Whether a search engine really followed a link. The tool reports what the page asks for.

### FAQ

**What is the difference between dofollow and nofollow links?**
A dofollow link is a normal link: search engines can follow it and treat it as a recommendation of the page it points to. A nofollow link carries `rel="nofollow"` (or `sponsored` or `ugc`), which asks search engines not to follow it or pass ranking credit through it.

**How do I check if a backlink is dofollow?**
Enter the address of the page that links to you and click **Check links**. Then type your domain in the backlink box. The tool lists each link to your site and labels it Followed, Nofollow, Sponsored or UGC.

**Are sponsored and UGC links nofollow?**
In effect, yes. Google introduced `sponsored` for paid links and `ugc` for user-generated content in 2019, and says links marked with any of the three values will generally not be followed. The tool counts all three as nofollow and shows which value each link uses.

**Why does the tool say all links are nofollow when they have no rel?**
The page has a robots meta tag with `nofollow` (or `none`). That applies to every link on the page at once. The tool shows the tag and marks such links “Nofollow (page)”.

**Should my internal links be nofollow?**
Usually not. Links between your own pages help search engines discover them and understand which matter most. The tool flags internal links that carry nofollow so you can decide.

**Where does the page get fetched from?**
Your browser asks the website directly. Most sites do not allow one website to read another, so the address is then sent to Jina Reader (r.jina.ai), which fetches the page. Only the address is sent. To avoid that, paste the HTML instead.

**Why are some links missing?**
They are probably added by JavaScript. Turn on **Run JavaScript first** and check again, or open the page, copy the HTML from your browser’s developer tools and paste it.

### Features

- **Readable glass, not just pretty glass**: Light text on light glass is the classic glassmorphism mistake. The contrast check follows the card as you drag it and suggests the tint opacity that makes text pass.
- **A real background**: Blur is only visible over something with edges. The backgrounds have colour blobs and sharp shapes, and you can drop in a screenshot of your own site.
- **Production-ready CSS**: Prefixed for older Safari, layered backgrounds one per line, fallbacks with a colour that keeps your text readable, and nothing you switched off.
- **Tailwind and React too**: Named Tailwind utilities where they exist (backdrop-blur-lg, rounded-3xl) and exact arbitrary values where they do not; React gets a style object with WebkitBackdropFilter.
- **Presets to start from**: Frosted, dark glass, colour tint, acrylic with grain and smoke — each one readable on its background.
- **Private**: Everything runs in your browser. Your photo is never uploaded, and your settings are saved only on this device.

### How to make a glassmorphism effect in CSS

1. **Pick a preset** — Start from **Frosted**, **Dark glass**, **Colour tint**, **Acrylic** or **Smoke**.
2. **Choose a background** — Try the built-in backgrounds, or **Use your own photo** — a screenshot of the page where the glass will sit is best.
3. **Adjust the glass** — Set the tint and its opacity, the blur and saturation, the corners, border, shadow, sheen and grain. Drag the card around the preview.
4. **Check the text** — Read the contrast line under the preview. If it is below 4.5:1, use the suggested tint opacity or change the text colour.
5. **Copy the code** — Choose **CSS**, **Tailwind**, **React** or **Demo page**, then **Copy** or **Download**.

### Guide

#### What glassmorphism is

Glassmorphism is a style of interface where cards, menus and panels look like frosted glass: you can see colours and shapes behind them, softly blurred, while text on top stays sharp. Apple uses it across macOS and iOS, Windows calls its version acrylic, and it became a web design trend in 2020.

In CSS the effect comes from one property, `backdrop-filter`, which blurs whatever is behind an element. It only shows when the element’s own background is partly transparent — a solid background hides the blur completely.

#### The CSS behind the effect

| Property | Typical value | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `background` | `rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.25)` | the tint: a see-through colour; lower opacity shows more of the background |
| `backdrop-filter` | `blur(16px) saturate(180%)` | blurs what is behind; saturation above 100% makes those colours richer |
| `-webkit-backdrop-filter` | the same | the same, for Safari before version 18 |
| `border` | `1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.45)` | a light edge that separates the glass from the background |
| `box-shadow` | `0 6px 21px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.14)` | lifts the card; an inset line can add a bright top edge |
| `border-radius` | `24px` | rounded corners, typical of glass surfaces |

#### Keeping text readable on glass

Text on glass sits on a background that changes from place to place, so it can be readable in one corner and not in another. WCAG 2 asks for a contrast of at least **4.5:1** for normal text and **3:1** for large text. This tool measures the glass over the whole card and reports the weakest spot.

If text is hard to read, raise the tint opacity, blur more (which evens out the background), switch between dark and light text, or give the text its own slightly darker or lighter panel.

#### Browser support

Figures from MDN’s browser compatibility data, October 2026. Browsers without the media query simply ignore it, so the fallback is safe to keep.

| Browser | backdrop-filter | prefers-reduced-transparency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chrome and Edge | since version 76 | since version 118 |
| Firefox | since version 103 | behind a setting only |
| Safari (macOS and iOS) | since 18; with `-webkit-` since 9 | not supported |

### FAQ

**Why does my backdrop-filter blur not show?**
Usually because the element’s background is solid — the blur is behind it, so make the background partly transparent. Also check that there is something behind the element to blur. If a parent element has its own filter, opacity below 1, a mask or a backdrop-filter, the specification says the blur only sees what is inside that parent (it calls this the backdrop root).

**Do I still need -webkit-backdrop-filter?**
Only for Safari 17 and older, which understood the prefixed name only. Safari 18 and every current Chrome, Edge and Firefox read `backdrop-filter`. Keeping both lines costs nothing, so the tool writes both.

**How do I make glassmorphism in Tailwind CSS?**
Use a semi-transparent background, a backdrop blur and a light border, for example `bg-white/25 backdrop-blur-lg backdrop-saturate-180 border border-white/45 rounded-3xl`. Open the **Tailwind** tab to get the classes for your exact settings.

**Is glassmorphism bad for performance?**
backdrop-filter makes the browser redraw what is behind the element whenever it changes, which costs more on large areas, big blur values and older phones. Use it on cards, menus and dialogs rather than whole pages, and avoid stacking many glass layers on top of each other.

**What is the difference between glassmorphism and neumorphism?**
Glassmorphism is see-through: a blurred view of what is behind. Neumorphism is solid: soft light and dark shadows make an element look pressed out of, or into, the same coloured surface. Try the [CSS Neumorphism Generator](https://justtools.online/css-tools/neumorphism-generator/) for that look.

**What does “Reduce transparency” do with my glass?**
Some people switch on Reduce transparency because see-through surfaces are tiring or hard to read. With **Add fallbacks** on, the CSS gives them a solid surface through the `prefers-reduced-transparency` media query, in a colour that keeps your text readable.

**Can it make Apple’s “Liquid Glass” look?**
Not the bending of light at the edges: that needs an SVG displacement filter inside backdrop-filter, which for now works only in Chromium browsers such as Chrome and Edge. This tool makes the frosted glass that works in every current browser, and the bright top edge and sheen give some of the same feel.

**Is my photo uploaded?**
No. The photo is read by your browser to show it behind the glass and to measure contrast, and it is never sent anywhere or saved. Your slider settings are kept in this browser’s local storage only.

### How to make a neumorphism effect in CSS

2. **Choose the shape** — **Flat** and **Convex** look pressed out, **Concave** looks scooped, **Pressed** looks pushed in.
3. **Set the light** — Click a direction or drag on the preview. Then adjust **Distance**, **Blur** and **Intensity** — a blur about twice the distance looks softest.
4. **Check the edges** — Read the checks under the preview. Switch on **Visible edge** for buttons and inputs, and use the suggested text colour if yours is too faint.
5. **Copy the code** — Copy the **CSS** or **Tailwind** classes for one element, or the **UI kit** for a full set of controls.

### Guide

#### How neumorphism works

Neumorphism (new skeuomorphism, or soft UI) makes elements look moulded from the background itself. The element has the same colour as the surface behind it, and two shadows shape it: a dark one on the side away from the light and a light one on the side facing it.

In CSS that is a single `box-shadow` with two values, such as `16px 16px 32px #bfc3ca, -16px -16px 32px #ffffff`. The word `inset` in front of both turns the shape into a hollow; a gradient background makes it convex or concave.

#### The four shapes

| Shape | Background | Shadow | Looks like |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Flat | the surface colour | outside | a raised, flat-topped tile |
| Convex | gradient, light side lighter | outside | a domed button |
| Concave | gradient, light side darker | outside | a raised dish |
| Pressed | the surface colour | inset | a hole or a pushed-in button |

#### Making neumorphism accessible

- WCAG 2.1 asks for **3:1** contrast for the visual boundary of buttons, inputs and other controls (success criterion 1.4.11). Soft shadows rarely reach it, so add a border to anything people must find and use — **Visible edge** does this with a colour that passes.
- Text needs **4.5:1** against the surface (3:1 for large text). Grey-on-grey text is the most common neumorphism mistake.
- Do not rely on the pressed look alone to show that a toggle is on; add a label, an icon or a colour change.
- Windows High Contrast mode removes box-shadows. The CSS adds a border inside `@media (forced-colors: active)` so every element still has an outline.
- Keep a visible focus ring for keyboard users; the tool’s button states include one.

### FAQ

**Why does neumorphism not work on a white background?**
The light shadow has to be lighter than the surface, and nothing is lighter than white — so the top edge disappears. Use a light grey such as `#e0e5ec` or `#f0f0f3` instead; the tool warns you when the surface is too light or too dark.

**How do I make a neumorphic button pressed when clicked?**
Give the button an inset version of its shadow in `:active`, for example `.neu:active { box-shadow: inset 9.6px 9.6px 19.2px #bfc3ca, inset -9.6px -9.6px 19.2px #ffffff; }`. With **Button states** on, the tool writes this for you, plus a focus ring and a smooth transition.

**How do I do neumorphism in Tailwind CSS?**
Use arbitrary values: a background the same as the page, such as `bg-[#e0e5ec]`, and a shadow like `shadow-[16px_16px_32px_#bfc3ca,-16px_-16px_32px_#ffffff]`. The **Tailwind** tab gives you the exact classes for your settings, including `active:` and `focus-visible:` states.

**Can neumorphism work in dark mode?**
Yes. Choose a dark surface such as `#2b2f36` and raise the intensity a little, because shadows show less on dark colours. Use light text and check its contrast in the panel under the preview.

**Is neumorphism bad for accessibility?**
It can be, because the shapes are drawn only with subtle shadows. It works when you add a visible border to controls, keep text contrast at 4.5:1 or more, and never use the pressed look as the only sign of state. The tool checks the first two for you.

**What is the difference between concave and convex?**
Both are raised from the surface. Convex has a gradient that is lighter on the side facing the light, so it bulges like a dome; concave has the opposite gradient, so it looks like a shallow dish.

**Are my settings saved?**
They are kept in this browser’s local storage so they are still there next time. Nothing is uploaded.

### Guide

#### What a bento grid is

A bento grid arranges content in tiles of different sizes inside one rectangle, like the compartments of a Japanese bento lunch box. A large tile carries the main message and smaller ones hold details, stats or images. Apple’s product pages made the style popular, and it now appears on portfolios, landing pages and dashboards.

CSS Grid is made for it: one container with `display: grid`, columns of equal width, and each tile told how many columns and rows to span.

#### How the generated CSS works

`grid-auto-rows: minmax(…, auto)` gives every row a minimum height but lets it grow when a tile has more content, so text is never cut off.

| Screen | Columns | How tiles are placed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phone (under 640 px) | your phone setting, usually 1 | one after another in reading order; tall tiles keep their height |
| Tablet (640–1023 px) | your tablet setting, usually 2 | spans shrunk to fit, in reading order |
| Desktop (1024 px and up) | as drawn | exactly where you drew them, with `grid-template-areas` or line numbers |

#### Bento layouts that work for everyone

- Keep the HTML in the order people should read it. This tool writes tiles left to right, top to bottom, exactly as you see them on desktop.
- `grid-auto-flow: dense` fills holes by moving later tiles up. That can make the order on screen differ from the order a keyboard or screen reader follows — fine for pictures, not for links and buttons.
- Put the most important content in the biggest tile; it is also the first tile on phones.
- Give tiles enough contrast with the page background, and let text wrap instead of fixing tile heights.

### FAQ

**How do I make a bento grid in CSS?**
Use a grid container, for example `display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, minmax(0, 1fr)); gap: 16px;`, then give big tiles a span such as `grid-column: span 2; grid-row: span 2;`. Draw your layout here and the tool writes all of this, plus the rules for tablets and phones.

**What is grid-template-areas?**
A CSS property that lets you draw the layout in text: each quoted string is a row and each word is a cell, so `"hero hero stats"` puts the hero tile across two columns. A dot marks an empty cell. Each tile then gets `grid-area: hero;`.

**How do I make a bento grid with Tailwind CSS?**
Use `grid` with responsive column counts such as `grid-cols-1 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4`, a row height like `auto-rows-[minmax(180px,auto)]`, and spans on the tiles such as `row-span-2 sm:col-span-2`. The **Tailwind** tab gives you the exact classes for your layout.

**How does the layout change on mobile?**
On phones the tiles stack in reading order in the number of columns you choose (one by default). On tablets, wide tiles shrink to fit the tablet columns. Open the **Phone** and **Tablet** views to see it before you copy the code.

**Why are there holes in my tablet layout?**
In reading order, a wide tile sometimes cannot fit next to the tile before it, so it starts a new row and leaves a gap. Change the tile sizes or the tablet columns, or switch on **Fill holes on smaller screens**, which lets later tiles move up into the gaps.

**Can I edit the grid with a keyboard?**
Yes. Press Tab to reach a tile, then use the arrow keys to move it, Shift with the arrow keys to resize it, and Delete to remove it. **Add tile** puts a new tile in the first free cell.

**Is my layout saved?**
Yes, in this browser’s local storage, so it is still there when you come back. Nothing is uploaded.

### How to animate elements on scroll with CSS

1. **Choose what to animate** — **Reveal** elements as they scroll in, add **Parallax**, a **Progress bar** or a **Shrinking header**.
2. **Pick an effect** — Choose fade up, zoom, blur, a wipe or another effect, and adjust its distance, size, blur or angle.
3. **Choose how it plays** — **Follows the scroll** ties the animation to the scroll position; **Plays once in view** runs it once, with a duration, delay and stagger.
4. **Watch the preview** — Scroll inside the preview box, or press **Replay**. Change the range until it starts and finishes where you want.
5. **Add it to your page** — Copy the **CSS**, put the **HTML** tab’s head line in your <head>, add the class to your elements, and include the **JavaScript** if there is one.

### Guide

#### What scroll-driven animations are

A normal CSS animation runs over time. A scroll-driven animation runs over a scroll distance instead: `animation-timeline: view()` ties it to the element’s journey through the screen, and `animation-timeline: scroll()` ties it to how far the whole page has scrolled. Scroll down and the animation moves forward; scroll back up and it moves back.

`animation-range` says which part of that journey the animation covers. `entry 0% cover 40%` starts as the element’s top edge appears at the bottom of the screen and finishes when it is 40% of the way through its time on screen.

#### The range names

| Range | Covers the time when the element… |
| --- | --- |
| `entry` | comes into view at the bottom of the screen |
| `exit` | leaves at the top of the screen |
| `cover` | is at least partly on screen, from first to last pixel |
| `contain` | is completely on screen (or fills it, if it is taller than the screen) |
| `entry-crossing` | crosses the bottom edge of the screen |
| `exit-crossing` | crosses the top edge of the screen |

#### Browser support

Figures from MDN’s browser compatibility data, October 2026.

| Browser | Scroll-driven animations | What the generated code does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chrome and Edge | since version 115 | runs the CSS |
| Safari (macOS and iOS) | since version 26 | runs the CSS |
| Firefox | test builds only | runs the fallback script |
| Older browsers | no | runs the fallback script, or shows content without animation |

### FAQ

**Do scroll animations need JavaScript?**
Not in Chrome, Edge and Safari 26 or later: `animation-timeline` does it in CSS. Firefox only has it in test builds, so the tool adds a short optional script that does the same job there. **Plays once in view** always uses a small script, because only Chrome 146 and later can start an animation on scroll with CSS alone (`animation-trigger`).

**Why must animation-timeline come after the animation shorthand?**
The `animation` shorthand resets every animation property it does not mention, including `animation-timeline`. Written before the shorthand, the timeline would be thrown away and the animation would run on the clock instead. The generated CSS always puts it after.

**How do I make elements fade in on scroll?**
Choose **Reveal** and the **Fade up** effect, copy the CSS, and add `class="reveal"` to the elements. For a scroll-linked version that is all you need in Chrome, Edge and Safari; add the script and the head line for other browsers.

**Is this an alternative to AOS (Animate On Scroll)?**
Yes. AOS is a JavaScript library that adds classes as elements come into view. This tool writes the same kind of effect as a few lines of CSS — plus about 20 lines of script where needed — with nothing to install.

**What happens for people who prefer reduced motion?**
All movement sits inside `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`, so people who have asked their device to reduce motion see the content straight away with no animation. The reading progress bar still works, because it shows information rather than decoration.

**Will hidden elements stay invisible if the script fails?**
No. Elements are only hidden when the line in the page head has confirmed that the script will run, and in scroll-linked mode the hidden state exists only inside the animation itself. If anything fails, the content simply appears.

**Can I animate several elements one after another?**
Yes. With **Plays once in view**, set a **Stagger**: elements that come into view together start one after another. With **Follows the scroll**, each element already animates at its own position.

**Are my settings saved?**
Yes, in this browser’s local storage, so they are still there when you come back. Nothing is uploaded.

## Half-Life Calculator

URL: https://justtools.online/education-tools/half-life-calculator/
Category: Education Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-14

Free half-life calculator: find the amount left, starting amount, time or half-life with the working shown, plus carbon-14 dating and activity for 67 isotopes.

### At a glance

- Solves **N = N₀ × (½)^(t ÷ T½)** for any one of the four: the amount left, the starting amount, the time or the half-life — and accepts a decay constant λ or a mean life τ instead of the half-life.
- Shows **the working step by step**, a decay curve with a mark at every half-life, and a table of the amount after each of the first ten half-lives.
- Half-lives of **67 isotopes** — carbon-14, iodine-131, technetium-99m, uranium-238 and more — with their uncertainties, from **NUBASE2020**, the international evaluation published by the IAEA. Carbon-14’s half-life there is 5,700 ± 30 years.
- Carbon-14 dating gives both the **conventional radiocarbon age** that laboratories report (with Libby’s half-life of 5,568 years, by international convention) and the age with the real half-life.
- Converts between **mass, activity, atoms and moles** for any of the isotopes, with atomic masses from AME2020: one gram of radium-226 is 0.989 curie.
- Works with numbers far beyond a calculator’s range by keeping their logarithms, so it can tell you that 10⁻⁶⁷⁴⁵¹ of a sample is left rather than 0.

### Features

- **Solve for anything**: Choose what to find and fill in the rest. Units can differ: give the time in days and the half-life in hours, and the tool converts.
- **Working you can copy**: Every answer comes with the formula, the numbers put into it and each step to the result — the way a teacher would want it written.
- **Real isotope data**: Pick an isotope and its half-life, uncertainty, decay mode, daughter and everyday use appear, all from the current international evaluation.
- **Carbon dating done properly**: See the radiocarbon age a laboratory would report and the age with the true half-life, and why the two differ.
- **Activity and mass**: How many becquerels is a microgram of iodine-131? How many atoms in 1 GBq of technetium-99m? Convert in either direction, with specific activity.
- **Free and private**: Everything is worked out in your browser. No sign-up, and your last inputs are remembered on this device only.

### How to calculate half-life problems

1. **Choose what to find** — Pick **Amount left**, **Starting amount**, **Time** or **Half-life**.
2. **Pick an isotope (optional)** — Choose one from the list, such as **C-14** or **I-131**, to fill in its half-life — or type your own.
3. **Enter the other values** — Use the same unit for both amounts (grams, atoms, becquerels or %). The time and half-life can use different units.
4. **Read the answer and the working** — The answer appears at once, with the fraction left, half-lives passed, decay constant and mean life, then the working step by step.
5. **Check with the curve and table** — The decay curve marks your point, and the table lists the amount after each half-life.

### Guide

#### The half-life formulas

| To find | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Amount left | `N = N₀ × (½)^(t ÷ T½)` |
| Starting amount | `N₀ = N × 2^(t ÷ T½)` |
| Time passed | `t = T½ × log₂(N₀ ÷ N)` |
| Half-life | `T½ = t × ln 2 ÷ ln(N₀ ÷ N)` |
| Decay constant | `λ = ln 2 ÷ T½ ≈ 0.693 ÷ T½` |
| Mean life | `τ = 1 ÷ λ = T½ ÷ ln 2 ≈ 1.443 × T½` |
| Activity | `A = λ × N` |

#### A worked example

Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8.0249 days. How much of a 400 MBq dose is left after 24 days? The time is 24 ÷ 8.0249 = 2.991 half-lives, so the amount left is 400 × (½)^2.991 = 50.3 MBq — just over an eighth, because three half-lives would take 24.07 days.

And how long until only 1 % is left? t = 8.0249 × log₂(100) = 8.0249 × 6.644 = 53.3 days. A rule of thumb follows from this: after 7 half-lives less than 1 % remains, and after 10 less than 0.1 %.

#### Half-lives of common isotopes

| Isotope | Half-life (NUBASE2020) | Known for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fluorine-18 | 109.734 minutes | PET scans |
| Technetium-99m | 6.0066 hours | medical imaging |
| Iodine-131 | 8.0249 days | thyroid treatment |
| Radon-222 | 3.8215 days | radon in homes |
| Cobalt-60 | 5.2714 years | radiotherapy |
| Caesium-137 | 30.04 years | fallout |
| Carbon-14 | 5,700 years | radiocarbon dating |
| Uranium-238 | 4.463 billion years | dating the oldest rocks |

### FAQ

**What is a half-life?**
The time it takes for half of the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay. It never changes: whether you start with a gram or a tonne, and whatever has already decayed, half of what is left decays in each half-life.

**How do I calculate the half-life from two measurements?**
Use `T½ = t × ln 2 ÷ ln(N₀ ÷ N)`. For example, if a count rate falls from 800 to 100 in 15 hours, N₀ ÷ N = 8 = 2³, so three half-lives passed and the half-life is 5 hours. Choose **Half-life** in the calculator to get the working.

**What is the difference between half-life, decay constant and mean life?**
They describe the same thing. The decay constant λ is the chance per unit time that one atom decays; the half-life is ln 2 ÷ λ; the mean life — the average time an atom survives — is 1 ÷ λ, about 1.443 half-lives. The calculator accepts any of the three.

**Why do radiocarbon labs use 5,568 years instead of 5,700?**
Radiocarbon dating began with Willard Libby’s value of 5,568 years. To keep every published result comparable, laboratories still report conventional radiocarbon ages with it (an international convention since 1977) and then convert them to calendar years with a calibration curve such as IntCal20, which also corrects for the true half-life and the changing amount of carbon-14 in the air.

**Does a sample ever decay completely?**
In theory the amount only halves, so it never reaches zero; in practice a sample is effectively gone after about 50 half-lives, when fewer than one atom in a thousand million million is left. With a small number of atoms, the last ones decay at random times.

**Can I use this for medicines, caffeine or other exponential decay?**
Yes — the formula is the same for anything that halves at a steady rate, such as how a drug is cleared from the body. Leave the isotope empty and type the half-life. Medicine half-lives vary from person to person, so ask a doctor or pharmacist about your own dose.

**Where do the half-lives come from?**
From NUBASE2020 (Kondev and others, Chinese Physics C, 2021), the evaluation of nuclear properties published by the IAEA’s Atomic Mass Data Center. It uses 1 year = 365.2422 days, and so does this calculator.

## Radioactive Decay Simulator

URL: https://justtools.online/education-tools/radioactive-decay-simulator/
Category: Education Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-14

Free radioactive decay simulator: watch up to 10,000 atoms decay at random, compare with the half-life curve, explore decay chains and do the dice experiment.

### At a glance

- Simulates **100 to 10,000 atoms**. Each atom draws the exact moment it decays from the exponential distribution, so the result does not depend on the frame rate or the speed you choose.
- Pick any of **67 isotopes** with their NUBASE2020 half-lives — from polonium-214 (164 microseconds) to uranium-238 (4.463 billion years) — and set how much time one second on screen stands for.
- Shows the counted atoms against the **expected curve** with a ±1 standard deviation band, and **measures the half-life** back from the run.
- Three real **decay chains**: strontium-90 → yttrium-90 (secular equilibrium), tellurium-132 → iodine-132 (transient equilibrium) and radon-222 with its short-lived products; or make your own parent and daughter. Expected numbers come from the Bateman equations.
- A **dice and coins** mode recreates the classroom experiment: remove every die that shows a six and the half-life is 3.8 throws; with coins it is exactly one toss.
- Optional **Geiger counter clicks**, an activity view, a log scale and a CSV download of every count for your own graphs.

### Features

- **Randomness you can see**: No atom knows when it will decay, yet thousands of them halve on schedule. The flashing squares and the wobbling line show both at once.
- **Exact, not stepped**: Decay times are drawn for each atom, so a fast or slow speed, or a slow computer, never changes the physics.
- **Decay chains and equilibrium**: See a daughter isotope build up until it decays as fast as it is made — the idea behind radon in homes and medical isotope generators.
- **The classroom experiment**: Run the dice, coin or 20-sided-dice experiment with up to 1,000 objects, throw by throw, with the table a worksheet asks for.
- **Real data**: Half-lives, decay modes and daughters come from NUBASE2020, the international evaluation published by the IAEA.
- **Data to take away**: Download every count as a CSV file and plot it in a spreadsheet, or fit the half-life yourself.

### How to use the radioactive decay simulator

1. **Choose what to simulate** — Pick **An isotope**, **A decay chain**, or **Dice or coins** for the classroom version.
2. **Choose the isotope and atoms** — Select an isotope such as **Ba-137m** or **I-131**, and the number of atoms — more atoms give a smoother curve.
3. **Start the clock** — Press **Start**. Each square changes colour when its atom decays; set the **Speed** to show more or less time per second.
4. **Compare with theory** — Watch the counted line against the dashed expected curve. Switch the chart to **Activity** or a **Log scale** — on a log scale decay is a straight line.
5. **Measure and download** — Read the half-life measured from your run, then download the numbers as a CSV file.

### Guide

#### Why decay is random but predictable

A radioactive nucleus has a fixed chance of decaying in any second, the decay constant λ, and nothing — not its age, temperature or neighbours — changes it. Which atom goes next is pure chance. But with many atoms the law of large numbers takes over: in each half-life about half of those left decay, and the count follows N = N₀ × (½)^(t ÷ T½).

The smaller the sample, the larger the wobble. The typical difference from the expected number is √(N₀ × p × (1 − p)), where p is the fraction expected to be left — about 16 atoms out of 1,000 after one half-life, but only 1.6 % of the sample instead of 5 % with ten times fewer atoms.

#### The decay chains

| Chain | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| Strontium-90 (28.91 years) → yttrium-90 (64.05 hours) → zirconium-90 | secular equilibrium: after about a month the two activities are equal |
| Tellurium-132 (3.204 days) → iodine-132 (2.295 hours) → xenon-132 | transient equilibrium: iodine-132 settles 3 % above its parent’s activity and falls with it |
| Radon-222 (3.8215 days) → polonium-218 → lead-214 → bismuth-214 → polonium-214 → lead-210 | the short-lived products of radon reach equilibrium in about three hours |
| Your own parent and daughter | try a daughter that lives longer than its parent: then no equilibrium forms |

#### Dice and coins as atoms

The half-life in throws is ln 2 ÷ −ln(1 − p), where p is the chance of removal in one throw.

| Object | Removed when | Chance per throw | Half-life |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Coin | it lands heads | 1 in 2 | 1 throw |
| Six-sided die | it shows a six | 1 in 6 | 3.80 throws |
| 20-sided die | it shows a 20 | 1 in 20 | 13.5 throws |

### FAQ

**Can you predict when a single atom will decay?**
No. Only the chance is known: an atom of iodine-131 has a 50 % chance of decaying within the next 8.0249 days, however long it has already existed. That is why the squares change colour in no pattern at all.

**Why does my simulation not match the curve exactly?**
Because decay is random. The count wanders around the expected curve, usually staying within the shaded ±1 standard deviation band. Use more atoms and the wander becomes smaller compared with the sample.

**What is secular equilibrium?**
When a long-lived parent decays into a much shorter-lived daughter, the daughter builds up until it decays as fast as it is made. From then on both have the same activity. Choose the strontium-90 chain and the **Activity** view to see it.

**How does the dice experiment model radioactive decay?**
Each die is an atom and each throw a tick of time. Every die has the same 1-in-6 chance of being removed, whatever happened before, just as every atom has the same chance of decaying. The number left falls exponentially, halving every 3.8 throws.

**Is the simulation accurate for real isotopes?**
Yes. Each atom’s decay time is drawn from the exponential distribution with the isotope’s NUBASE2020 half-life, and the decay chains are checked against the Bateman equations. The only simplification is that branches below 0.03 % in the radon chain are left out.

**Can I use the results for homework?**
Yes. Download the CSV and plot the counts against time, or ln(counts) against time to get a straight line whose slope is −λ. The tool shows its own estimate of the half-life so you can check yours.

### Guide

#### Ways to show a molecule

| Style | What it shows | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ball and stick | atoms as small balls, bonds as sticks | seeing bonds and angles |
| Sticks | bonds only, coloured by atom | crowded molecules |
| Space-filling | atoms at their van der Waals size | the real shape and bulk of a molecule |

#### What the colours mean

Atoms are coloured with the CPK convention, in the shades used by Jmol and most viewers:

### FAQ

**Which file formats can I open?**
PDB (.pdb, .ent), mmCIF (.cif), SDF and MOL (.sdf, .mol, V2000 and V3000), MOL2, XYZ, PQR and GROMACS (.gro). You can also paste the text of a file. Files are read in your browser and never uploaded.

**Where do the 3D shapes of small molecules come from?**
From PubChem, which computes a low-energy 3D conformer for most small organic compounds. It is a calculated shape, not a measured one. PubChem has no 3D shape for compounds that are too large, too flexible or contain elements its method does not cover (such as most metals); for those the viewer shows the flat 2D drawing and says so.

**Why are there no hydrogen atoms in my protein?**
X-ray crystallography rarely sees hydrogen atoms, so most PDB entries leave them out. The formula and molar mass then count only the atoms in the file, and the viewer tells you so.

**How do I measure a bond angle?**
Choose **Angle** under Measure and click three atoms, with the middle atom second. For a bond length choose **Distance** and click two atoms; for a torsion choose **Torsion** and click four atoms along the chain.

**What do the purple clouds mean?**
They are lone pairs: pairs of electrons on the central atom that are not in a bond. VSEPR theory says they push the bonds apart, which is why water is bent and ammonia is a pyramid. Switch them off with **Lone pairs**.

**Can I use the pictures in my slides or homework?**
Yes. Use **Picture** to save a PNG. Structures from the Protein Data Bank are free to use (CC0); mention the PDB ID. PubChem asks you to cite it as the source of its data.

**Does it work on a phone?**
Yes. Drag with one finger to turn the molecule and pinch to zoom. Very large proteins can be slow on older phones — the Wire or Cartoon styles are the lightest.

**What is sent over the internet?**
Only what you search for: names, SMILES and CIDs go to PubChem (run by the US National Library of Medicine), PDB IDs to the RCSB Protein Data Bank. The built-in molecules and the files you open do not leave your device.

## CSS Box Shadow Generator

URL: https://justtools.online/css-tools/box-shadow-generator/
Category: CSS Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-15

Free CSS box-shadow generator: build smooth layered shadows, edit each layer, start from Tailwind or Material presets, and copy CSS, Tailwind or React.

### At a glance

- **Smooth mode** stacks up to 8 shadow layers, each twice as far and as soft as the one before, so the shadow fades the way a real one does instead of ending in one grey blur.
- The shadow can take its **colour from the background** — a dark shade of the same hue — which looks more natural than black on coloured pages.
- A **layer editor** for x, y, blur, spread, colour, opacity and inset, with show/hide, duplicate and reorder. The first layer in the list is drawn on top.
- **27 presets**: eight designs, the 10 shadow and inset-shadow utilities of Tailwind CSS v4 and the 9 Material Design elevations (1 to 24 dp).
- **Paste any box-shadow** — hex, rgb(), hsl() or a colour name, with or without `box-shadow:` — to see it and edit it. Anything it cannot read is explained.
- Copy **CSS** (with an optional hover lift that respects reduced motion), **Tailwind v4 classes** checked against Tailwind’s compiler, a **React** style, a **drop-shadow() filter** or five **elevation tokens** as CSS variables.

### Features

- **Shadows that look real**: One big blur looks flat. Layered shadows put a sharp, dark shadow near the element and a wide, faint one far away, like light in a room.
- **Every layer in reach**: Pick any layer to change it, hide it to compare, duplicate it to build on it, or move it up. The CSS updates as you drag.

- **Edit what you already have**: Paste a shadow from your stylesheet, a design tool or a framework and it opens in the layer editor.

- **Private**: Everything runs in your browser. Your settings are saved only on this device.

### How to make a box shadow in CSS

1. **Choose how to start** — Use **Smooth** for a soft layered shadow, **Presets** for Tailwind, Material or a ready design, or **Paste CSS** to edit a shadow you have.
2. **Shape the shadow** — In Smooth, set where the light comes from, the distance, softness, number of layers and opacity. In **Layers**, choose a layer and change its offsets, blur, spread, colour and opacity.
3. **Check it in place** — Set the background, element colour, corner radius and shape to match your page, and try the **Dark** preview.
4. **Add a hover state** — Switch on **Lift on hover** for a deeper shadow and a small lift when the element is pointed at.
5. **Copy the code** — Choose **CSS**, **Tailwind**, **React**, **drop-shadow** or **Elevation tokens**, then **Copy** or **Download**.

### Guide

#### How box-shadow works

The CSS `box-shadow` property draws one or more shadows around an element’s box, following its rounded corners. Each shadow is written as up to four lengths and a colour, with the word `inset` to put it inside the element. Separate several shadows with commas; the first one is drawn on top.

| Part | Example | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| x offset | `0` | moves the shadow right (negative: left) |
| y offset | `8px` | moves the shadow down (negative: up) |
| blur | `24px` | how soft the edge is; 0 is a hard edge, and it cannot be negative |
| spread | `-4px` | grows the shadow (or shrinks it, if negative) before the blur |
| colour | `rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.12)` | usually a dark, see-through colour; without one, the text colour is used |
| `inset` | `inset 0 2px 4px …` | draws the shadow inside the element, so it looks pressed in |

#### Why layered shadows look better

A real shadow is sharp and dark close to an object and gets wider and fainter further away. One `box-shadow` layer can only do one of those at a time, so it looks either harsh or muddy. Stacking a few layers, each with double the offset and blur of the last, gets much closer — the idea Josh W. Comeau and Tobias Ahlin popularised as smooth or layered shadows.

Tinting helps too. A shadow on a blue page is not grey; it is a darker, duller blue. With **Colour from the background** on, the tool works out that colour for you in the OKLCH colour space.

#### Tailwind CSS v4 shadow values

From Tailwind CSS v4.3’s default theme. In v4, the old `shadow-sm` is now `shadow-xs` and the old `shadow` is now `shadow-sm`, so check the names when you upgrade from v3.

| Class | box-shadow |
| --- | --- |
| `shadow-2xs` | `0 1px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.05)` |
| `shadow-xs` | `0 1px 2px 0 rgb(0 0 0 / 0.05)` |
| `shadow-sm` | `0 1px 3px 0 rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1), 0 1px 2px -1px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1)` |
| `shadow-md` | `0 4px 6px -1px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1), 0 2px 4px -2px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1)` |
| `shadow-lg` | `0 10px 15px -3px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1), 0 4px 6px -4px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1)` |
| `shadow-xl` | `0 20px 25px -5px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1), 0 8px 10px -6px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.1)` |
| `shadow-2xl` | `0 25px 50px -12px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.25)` |

#### box-shadow or drop-shadow()?

`box-shadow` always follows the element’s box. `filter: drop-shadow()` follows the visible shape instead — the outline of a transparent PNG, an SVG icon or text. It has no spread and no inset, and several drop-shadows are applied one after another, so each one also shadows the shadow before it. Use the **drop-shadow** tab for images and icons, and box-shadow for cards, buttons and panels.

### FAQ

**How do I add more than one box shadow?**
Separate the shadows with commas in one `box-shadow` declaration, for example `box-shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1), 0 8px 24px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.12);`. A second `box-shadow` line would replace the first instead of adding to it. The first shadow in the list is drawn on top.

**How do I put a shadow on only one side?**
Offset the shadow towards that side and use a negative spread to pull the other edges in. For a shadow only at the bottom, try `0 8px 6px -6px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.3)`. For one inside edge, use inset, as in `inset 0 2px 0 rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)` for the top.

**What is the difference between blur and spread?**
Spread changes the size of the shadow — positive spread makes it bigger than the element, negative makes it smaller. Blur then softens its edge; a blur of 0 gives a hard edge. A shadow with 0 offsets, 0 blur and 1px spread draws a 1px line around the element, which is a common way to make a border that takes no space.

**Why does my shadow look grey and dirty?**
Usually because it is one large, dark layer of pure black. Use several lighter layers instead (Smooth mode does this), keep each layer’s opacity low, and tint the shadow towards the background colour rather than black.

**How do I make shadows in Tailwind CSS?**
Use the built-in utilities such as `shadow-sm`, `shadow-md` or `shadow-lg`, or an arbitrary value for anything else — spaces become underscores, as in `shadow-[0_8px_24px_rgba(0,0,0,0.12)]`. The **Tailwind** tab writes the right one for your shadow, and the class names are for Tailwind v4.

**Do box shadows work on dark backgrounds?**
They are much harder to see, because there is little light to take away. On dark pages, raise the opacity, make the element lighter than the background, or add a faint light ring such as `0 0 0 1px rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.06)`. Use the **Dark** preview to check.

**Are box shadows bad for performance?**
Static shadows are cheap. Animating `box-shadow` itself makes the browser repaint each frame, which can stutter on large elements or slow phones. For many animated cards, put the hover shadow on a pseudo-element and animate its opacity instead.

**Which browsers support box-shadow?**
All of them. Every browser in use today supports box-shadow without a prefix, including multiple and inset shadows; the `-webkit-box-shadow` prefix has not been needed for over ten years.

| 24 megapixels | 6000 × 4000 px | 101.6 × 67.7 cm |
| 48 megapixels | 8000 × 6000 px | 135.5 × 101.6 cm |

#### Tips for a neat poster

- Print a single test sheet first and check that the 10 cm line really measures 10 cm.
- Turn off borderless printing and any “fit”, “shrink” or “scale to page” option.
- Heavier paper (100–120 g/m²) or matte photo paper wrinkles less under glue.
- Trim with a metal ruler and a craft knife; scissors leave wavy edges that show at the joins.
- Use a glue stick or double-sided tape in the overlap strips; wet glue makes paper ripple.
- Join each row first, then join the rows – it is easier to keep long edges straight.

### FAQ

**How do I print one picture on several pages?**
Add the picture here, choose how many sheets across it should be (or its final size), then press **Make poster PDF**. The PDF has one page per sheet; print them all at actual size and join them in the order of their names – A1, A2, then B1, B2 and so on.

**Why don’t my printed sheets line up?**
Almost always because the print dialog scaled the pages: “Fit to page” or “Shrink to printable area” makes each sheet slightly smaller. Choose **Actual size** or **100 %** and check the 10 cm line on the guide page. If it is still off, set the printer margin in the tool to at least what your printer needs.

**What printer margin should I use?**
Most inkjet and laser printers need 3–6 mm on each side. The default of 10 mm is safe for almost every printer and leaves room for the sheet names. Your printer’s manual or its “borderless” settings tell you the exact minimum.

**How many A4 pages make an A1 poster?**
An A1 sheet has the area of 8 A4 sheets, but because each page loses its margins and shares an overlap with its neighbours you need more: 15 A4 sheets with 10 mm margins and 10 mm overlap, or 9 with 5 mm margins and no overlap.

**Can I print a PDF poster on A4 sheets?**
Yes. Choose the PDF and the page; the page is copied into each sheet as vector graphics, so text and lines stay crisp at any size. A password-protected PDF can be opened with its password, which is used only on your device.

**What is rasterbation?**
It is the name the Rasterbator gave to making huge posters out of halftone dots. Choose the **Dots** style: each dot is as big as the picture is dark at that spot, in black, in the picture’s own colours, or in one colour of your choice. Seen from a few metres away the dots merge into the picture.

**Is my picture uploaded?**
No. The picture or PDF is opened and laid out by your browser, and the poster PDF is made on your device. Only your size and paper settings are saved, in this browser.

## Online Teleprompter

URL: https://justtools.online/text-tools/online-teleprompter/
Category: Text Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-15

Free online teleprompter: paste your script, set the speed or let it follow your voice, mirror it for glass and record yourself on camera. No sign-up.

### At a glance

- Scrolls the script at a steady speed set in **words per minute** (60–260), shows how long the script takes to read, and lets you speed up or slow down while reading.
- **Follow my voice** listens through the microphone and keeps the word you are saying on the reading line, waiting when you pause and dimming what you have read.
- In Chrome and Edge, speech can be recognised **on your device** after a one-off language-pack download. Where that is not possible, voice following uses the browser’s online speech service only after you allow it.
- **Mirror** and **upside-down** modes for teleprompter glass, four high-contrast colour schemes, text up to 160 px and an adjustable reading line.
- Optional **camera behind the text**: see yourself while reading and record to an MP4 or WebM file on your device.
- Controlled by keyboard, **presentation clickers** and Bluetooth page turners, or by touch: tap to pause, drag to move. The screen is kept awake while you read.
- Scripts can have `#` sections to jump between with keys 1–9, `[stage directions]` that are shown but not read, and `**bold**` words. Your script and settings are saved only in this browser.

### Features

- **Reads at your pace**: Set the speed in words per minute, the way speakers think about pace, and see the total speaking time before you start.
- **Follows your voice**: Read aloud and the text keeps up, slowing when you slow down and stopping when you stop – no one needs to work the scroll.
- **Eye contact on camera**: Put the reading line near the top of the screen and narrow the text, so your eyes stay close to the webcam while you read.
- **Ready for real teleprompters**: Mirror the text for beam-splitter glass, flip it for upside-down rigs, and drive it with a clicker or Bluetooth remote.
- **Record yourself**: Turn on the camera to see yourself behind the words and record a take straight to your device – no upload, no watermark.
- **Private**: Your script stays in this browser. With on-device speech, not even your voice leaves your computer.

### How to use the online teleprompter

1. **Add your script** — Paste or type it, or **Open** a text file. Use `#` for section headings and `[brackets]` for notes to yourself.
2. **Choose how it moves** — Pick **Steady scroll** and a speed, or **Follow my voice** and your language.
3. **Set up the screen** — Choose the text size, colours and reading line; turn on **Mirror** for teleprompter glass or the camera to record yourself.
4. **Start** — Press **Start prompter**. After the countdown, read along; press Space to pause and the arrow keys to move or change speed.
5. **Finish** — Press Esc or ✕ to close. **Carry on** picks up where you stopped.

### Guide

#### How fast should a teleprompter scroll?

As fast as you speak naturally – which is why the speed here is set in words per minute rather than an abstract number. Start at the default of 140 and adjust with the arrow keys while reading; the prompter remembers your speed for next time.

| Delivery | Words per minute (about) | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slow and deliberate | 100–120 | speeches, training videos, reading in a second language |
| Presentation | 120–140 | talks, webinars, explainer videos |
| Conversational | 140–160 | YouTube, vlogs, interviews |
| Brisk | 160–190 | ads, news-style updates, short-form video |

#### Writing a script that reads well

- Write the way you talk: short sentences, everyday words, contractions.
- One idea per paragraph, with a blank line between them – the gaps are natural places to breathe.
- Spell out anything awkward to say: “twenty twenty-six”, “J-S-O-N”.
- Use `[pause]`, `[smile]` or `[show the product]` for directions you should not read aloud.
- Mark the few words to stress with `**stars**` – not whole sentences.
- Split long scripts into `#` sections, and record them as separate takes.

#### Keeping eye contact with a webcam

Viewers notice when your eyes drift down the screen. Put the reading line high (20–30 %), make the text column narrow (50–70 %) and sit far enough back that the lines are small movements for your eyes. On a laptop, a browser window placed just under the camera works better than full screen.

For a real teleprompter, a tablet lies under a sheet of beam-splitter glass in front of the lens. The glass reflects the screen, so turn on **Mirror the text** to read it the right way round.

### FAQ

**How does voice scrolling work?**
Your browser’s speech recognition turns what you say into words, and the prompter matches them against the script – allowing for misheard words, skipped words and numbers said aloud – then smoothly moves the word you are on to the reading line. If you go off-script, it waits until it hears a line it recognises.

**Is my voice sent anywhere?**
Not when your browser can recognise speech on the device, which the page tells you – Chrome and Edge can, for many languages, after downloading a speech pack once. Otherwise voice following only starts after you allow your browser’s online speech service (Google’s for Chrome, Microsoft’s for Edge, Apple’s for Safari), which receives the audio. JustTools itself never receives your voice or your script.

**Does it work on an iPad or phone?**
Yes. Steady scrolling, mirror mode, tap to pause and drag to scroll work in every modern mobile browser, and the screen is kept awake while you read. Voice following works in Safari and Chrome on iPhone and iPad, and in Chrome on Android.

**Can I control it with a remote?**
Yes. Presentation clickers and Bluetooth page turners send Page Down/Page Up or arrow keys, which move the script forward and back; their blank-screen button (B or .) starts and stops it. A Bluetooth keyboard works too – see the keyboard list under the Start button.

**Can I record myself while reading?**
Turn on **Camera behind the text**, start the prompter and press **Record**. When you stop, the video downloads to your device – as MP4 where the browser can make it (Chrome, Edge, Safari), otherwise WebM. Nothing is uploaded.

**Why is my text backwards?**
**Mirror the text** is on. That is for teleprompter glass, which reflects the screen; turn it off to read straight from the screen. Press M in the prompter to switch.

**Where is my script saved?**
In this browser’s local storage, on this device only, so it is still there next time you open the page. Clearing your browser data removes it.

## Online Notepad

URL: https://justtools.online/text-tools/online-notepad/

Free online notepad that saves as you type, right in your browser: many notes, search, find and replace, open and save text files, share by link. No sign-up.

### At a glance

- Saves as you type into your **browser’s own storage** (IndexedDB) – no account and no upload. Open the page again on the same device and your notes are there.
- Keep **any number of notes**: search across titles and text, pin the important ones, and get deleted notes back from the **trash** for 30 days.
- **Find and replace** with match case, whole words and regular expressions (with `$1` groups); every match is highlighted in the text.
- **Open text files** in UTF-8, UTF-16 or Windows-1252. In Chrome and Edge, **Ctrl+S saves back to the same file**; other browsers download a .txt or .md file.
- **Share a note as a link**: the text is compressed into the part of the link after #, which browsers never send to a web server.
- Notepad habits kept: **F5** types the time and date, a first line of **.LOG** adds a time stamp each time the note is opened, Tab types a tab, plus word wrap, font and size.
- Notes stay in step across open tabs. Back up everything as one JSON file, or download all notes as a ZIP of .txt files.

### Features

- **Nothing to lose**: There is no Save button to forget: each change is stored within a moment, and again when you close the tab or switch away.
- **Private by design**: Your notes are written to this browser only. There is no account, no server copy and no tracking of what you write.
- **Proper find and replace**: Highlights every match, steps through them with Enter, and replaces one or all – with regular expressions for the tricky jobs.
- **Works with your files**: Open .txt, .md, .csv, .log or code files, edit them, and save them back where they came from (Chrome and Edge) or download a copy.
- **Focus mode**: Hide everything but the page for distraction-free writing, in the font and size you like.
- **Yours to take away**: Back up all notes in one file and restore them on another computer or browser, or send a single note as a link.

### How to use the online notepad

1. **Start writing** — Type in the editor. The first line becomes the note’s title unless you give it one.
2. **Add more notes** — Press **New** (or Alt+N). Your notes are listed on the left – on a phone, under **Notes** – newest first.
3. **Find things** — Search the list to find a note, or press Ctrl+F to find (and Ctrl+H to replace) inside the one you are reading.
4. **Open and save files** — Use **Open** for a text file and **Save** (Ctrl+S) to write it to a file. More options are in the ⋯ menu.
5. **Keep a backup** — Now and then, choose **Back up everything** in the menu; **Restore or import** brings the notes back.

### Guide

#### Where are my notes kept?

In your browser, on this device: the notes go into IndexedDB, the browser’s built-in database for websites. They survive closing the tab and restarting the computer, and no one else can read them – including JustTools.

They are removed if you clear this site’s data or browsing history, and a private window forgets them when it closes. Browsers can also clear storage of sites you have not used for a long time when disk space runs low; **Protect notes from clean-up** in the menu asks the browser not to. For anything important, keep a backup file.

#### Keyboard shortcuts

On a Mac, use Cmd instead of Ctrl.

| Keys | Does |
| --- | --- |
| Ctrl + S | save to a file (back to the same file in Chrome and Edge) |
| Ctrl + O | open text files as new notes |
| Ctrl + F | find in the note |
| Ctrl + H | find and replace |
| Enter / Shift + Enter | next / previous match |
| Alt + N | new note |
| F5 | type the time and date |
| Ctrl + P | print the note |
| Esc, then Tab | leave the editor with the keyboard |

#### Regular expressions in find and replace

| Pattern | Matches | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `\d+` | a run of digits | order **1042** |
| `\w+@\w+\.\w+` | a simple e-mail address | **ana@site.com** |
| `^- ` | “- ” at the start of a line | list items |
| `\s+$` | spaces at the end of a line | trailing spaces |
| `(\d+)-(\d+)-(\d+)` | a date, in three groups | replace with `$3/$2/$1` |
| `colou?r` | colour or color | both spellings |

#### Sharing a note by link

**Share link** copies a link with the note inside it, compressed after the # sign. Browsers do not send that part of a link to the web server, so the note is not stored anywhere – it exists only in the link and wherever you paste it. Whoever opens the link sees the note and can save a copy to their own notes.

Anyone with the link can read the note, so share it the way you would share the text itself. Very long notes make very long links, which some chat apps cut short; send a file instead.

### FAQ

**Is this online notepad private?**
Yes. Notes are saved in your browser on this device and never sent to JustTools or anyone else. The only way a note leaves your device is if you download it, save it to a file, or copy a share link yourself.

**Will my notes still be here tomorrow?**
Yes, on the same device and browser, unless you clear this site’s data or use a private window. For safety, use **Protect notes from clean-up** and keep a backup with **Back up everything**.

**How do I move my notes to another computer?**
Choose **Back up everything (.json)** in the menu, copy the file to the other computer, open this page there and choose **Restore or import…**. Notes that already exist are kept unless the backup has a newer version.

**Can I edit a .txt file and save it back?**
Yes. Press **Open** (Ctrl+O) and choose the file. In Chrome and Edge, **Save** (Ctrl+S) writes your changes back to that same file after you allow it once. Firefox and Safari do not let websites write to files, so Save downloads a copy instead.

**What does .LOG do?**
It is a trick from Windows Notepad: if the first line of a note is exactly `.LOG`, the time and date are added at the end each time you open the note – handy for a diary or a work log. F5 types the time and date at the cursor.

**Does it work offline?**
Once the page has loaded, writing, saving and searching need no connection, because everything happens in your browser.

**Can I format text or use Markdown?**
This is a plain-text notepad, which keeps it fast and its files universal. You can write Markdown and download it as .md, or see it formatted in the [Markdown Previewer](https://justtools.online/developer-tools/markdown-previewer/).

## Attendance Calculator

URL: https://justtools.online/calculators/attendance-calculator/
Category: Calculators
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-15

Free attendance calculator: your attendance %, how many classes you can skip or must attend to reach 75%, subject-wise tracking and a term planner.

### At a glance

- Attendance % = classes attended ÷ classes held × 100. The calculator gives the **exact number of classes to attend in a row** to reach your minimum, or **how many you can miss** and stay at it.
- At **75%**, each class you miss has to be balanced by three you attend: 30 of 50 (60%) needs **30 more in a row**, while 45 of 50 (90%) can miss **10**.
- Works with any minimum – 75% (CBSE board exams and many colleges), 70% per subject (law, under the BCI rules), 75% theory and 80% practical (MBBS) – using exact whole-number arithmetic, so 75% of 40 is exactly 30.
- An option for colleges that **round to the nearest whole percent**, where 74.5% counts as 75%.
- Counts approved **medical, duty or OD leave** as present if your college does, and with the classes left this term says how many you must attend – or that the minimum can no longer be reached.
- **Subject-wise tracker** with one-tap Present and Absent buttons and Undo, the overall percentage, the subjects below the minimum and a CSV download.
- **Term planner**: enter classes per weekday, holidays and the last day of classes, then tick the days you plan to miss to see your percentage after every day. Everything is saved in your browser only.

### Features

- **The answer students want**: “You can miss the next 4 classes” or “Attend the next 12 in a row” – with the percentage before and after, and the working.
- **Every subject at a glance**: One row per subject with its percentage, a bar against your minimum and what it allows, plus the overall figure most colleges also check.
- **Tap after each class**: Present and Absent buttons keep the numbers current without retyping them; Undo fixes a wrong tap.
- **Plan the whole term**: From your timetable and holidays it lists every class day left, so you can see which days you can afford to miss – and which you cannot.
- **Any rule**: Set 60, 75, 80, 85% or any figure, and choose exact or rounded comparison to match your college’s handbook.
- **Private**: No sign-up and no upload: your numbers stay in this browser for the next time you check.

### How to calculate attendance and the classes you can skip

1. **Set your minimum** — Type your college’s requirement or tap 75%, 80% and so on. Choose **Rounded %** if your college rounds to whole percent.
2. **Enter your classes** — On **Calculator**, type the classes held and attended (or missed). Add leave counted as present and the classes left this term if you know them.
3. **Read the answer** — See your percentage, how many classes you can miss or must attend in a row, and the what-if table.
4. **Track each subject** — On **Subjects**, enter each subject’s numbers once, then tap **Present** or **Absent** after every class.
5. **Plan the term** — On **Term planner**, fill in your weekly timetable, holidays and the last day of classes, and tick the days you plan to miss.

### Guide

#### Attendance formulas

**Attendance % = attended ÷ held × 100.** To find how many classes you must attend in a row to reach a minimum p (as a fraction, 75% = 0.75), solve (attended + x) ÷ (held + x) ≥ p, which gives **x ≥ (p × held − attended) ÷ (1 − p)**, rounded up.

To find how many you can miss and still have p, solve attended ÷ (held + y) ≥ p, which gives **y ≤ attended ÷ p − held**, rounded down.

| You have | Attendance | At 75% | At 80% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30 of 50 | 60% | attend the next 30 | attend the next 50 |
| 36 of 50 | 72% | attend the next 6 | attend the next 20 |
| 40 of 50 | 80% | can miss 3 | can miss 0 |
| 45 of 50 | 90% | can miss 10 | can miss 6 |
| 54 of 60 | 90% | can miss 12 | can miss 7 |

#### How many classes can I miss?

The minimum decides how many classes you must attend for every one you miss. Over a whole term this is the largest share of classes you can miss:

| Minimum | Attend for every class missed | Most you can miss |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 60% | 1.5 | 40% of classes |
| 65% | 1.86 | 35% of classes |
| 70% | 2.33 | 30% of classes |
| 75% | 3 | 25% – 1 in 4 |
| 80% | 4 | 20% – 1 in 5 |
| 85% | 5.67 | 15% of classes |
| 90% | 9 | 10% – 1 in 10 |

#### Attendance rules you may meet

Colleges and universities set their own rules on top of these, often per subject and overall, and some count labs as two or more periods. Check your handbook – and count periods the same way it does.

| Where | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| CBSE Class 10 and 12 | 75% to sit the board exams (Examination Bye-Laws); shortages of up to 25% can be condoned for medical emergencies, national or international sport and other serious reasons, with documents |
| MBBS in India (NMC) | 75% in theory and 80% in practical and clinical training |
| Law degrees in India (BCI) | 70% in each subject; a college may condone down to 65% in a subject if the overall attendance is 70% |
| Schools in the United States | missing 10% or more of school days, excused or not, is “chronic absenteeism” |
| Schools in England | missing 10% or more of sessions (half days) is “persistent absence” |

#### If you are short of attendance

- Act early: every week left in the term is classes that can still pull the percentage up.
- Attend everything for a while – the What if table shows how fast the figure climbs.
- Get approved medical, sports or duty leave on record now, with documents; it is much harder afterwards.
- Ask how condonation works at your college: who decides, how far below the minimum is allowed, and the deadline.
- Watch each subject, not just the overall figure – one short subject can stop you sitting its exam.

### FAQ

**How do I calculate my attendance percentage?**
Divide the classes you attended by the classes held and multiply by 100. For example, 42 classes attended out of 56 held is 42 ÷ 56 × 100 = **75%**.

**How many classes can I miss and still have 75%?**
Divide the classes you have attended by 0.75 and subtract the classes held so far, then round down. With 45 of 50, that is 45 ÷ 0.75 − 50 = **10** classes. Enter your numbers above to get yours.

**How many classes do I need to attend to reach 75%?**
Use (0.75 × held − attended) ÷ 0.25, rounded up. With 30 of 50 (60%), you need (37.5 − 30) ÷ 0.25 = **30** classes in a row, which takes you to 60 of 80 = 75%.

**Does medical leave count as attendance?**
It depends on your institution. Many colleges add approved duty or on-duty (OD) leave to attendance, and some count medical leave or allow it when deciding condonation. Enter such classes under **Leave counted as present** only if your college counts them.

**Is the 75% rule per subject or overall?**
Often both: many universities require the minimum in each subject and overall, and a strong overall figure can hide one subject that is short. Use the **Subjects** tab to see every subject against the minimum.

**What if I can’t reach 75% this term?**
The calculator tells you when even attending every remaining class is not enough. Speak to your teacher or department straight away about medical or duty leave and condonation – most rules allow some relaxation only with documents and before a deadline.

**Are my numbers saved?**
Yes, in this browser on this device, so they are there next time. Nothing is sent anywhere, and you can clear them at any time.
