Play classic Klondike solitaire online free: draw 1 or draw 3, Vegas scoring, winnable deals, hints, undo and a daily deal. No download, no sign-up.

### At a glance

- Classic **Klondike** rules: build the seven columns down in alternating colours, and the four foundations up by suit from ace to king. Choose **Draw 1** (easier) or **Draw 3** (the classic challenge).
- **Winnable deals only**: before you see a deal, a built-in solver checks it can be won. Even knowing where every card is, only about **82%** of draw-three deals can be won (Blake and Gent, 2019).
- **Windows scoring** (10 for a card on a foundation, 5 for turning a card, a time bonus of 700,000 ÷ seconds), **Vegas** scoring ($52 for the deck, $5 a card back), or no score at all.
- **Tap a card** to send it where it fits, or drag it. Safe cards go up to the foundations by themselves, and **Finish** plays out the rest once every card is face up.
- Unlimited **undo**, **hints**, a **daily deal**, deals you can **share by number**, and a **Solve it for me** button that plays out a winning line.

### Features

- **Every deal can be won**: The solver tries each deal before you get it, so a loss is never the cards’ fault. Turn it off for random deals.
- **Plays the way you do**: Tap to move, drag and drop, or use the keyboard. Left-handed layout puts the stock on the right.
- **Help when you’re stuck**: Hints point to a useful move, undo has no limit, and the game tells you when no useful moves are left.
- **Windows or Vegas scoring**: The original Windows Solitaire points and time bonus, the Vegas money game with limited passes, or no score.
- **A deal a day**: The daily deal is the same for everyone today — and any game can be shared by its number.
- **The bouncing cards**: Win and the cards cascade off the foundations, just like the Windows classic.

### How to play solitaire

1. **Aim for the foundations** — Move all 52 cards to the four foundations at the top, one suit each, from ace up to king.
2. **Build down in the columns** — In the seven columns, put a card on one rank higher of the opposite colour — a red 6 on a black 7. You can move a whole run of cards together.
3. **Turn up hidden cards** — When you move the face-up cards off a column, the card below turns over. Only a king (or a run starting with one) can fill an empty column.
4. **Draw from the stock** — Tap the stock to turn one or three cards onto the waste. The top waste card can be played. When the stock runs out, tap again to turn the waste over.
5. **Win** — Once every card is face up, press **Finish** and the rest go up by themselves.

### Guide

#### Scoring

Standard scores never drop below zero. In Vegas scoring you get one pass through the stock when drawing one card and three passes when drawing three; your running Vegas total is kept with your stats.

| Move | Standard (Windows) | Vegas |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Card from the waste to a column | +5 | — |
| Card to a foundation | +10 | +$5 |
| Turning over a column card | +5 | — |
| Card from a foundation back to a column | −15 | −$5 |
| Turning the waste over (draw 1) | −100 | Not allowed |
| Time | −2 every 10 seconds; win bonus 700,000 ÷ seconds (30 s or more) | — |
| Start | 0 | −$52 |

#### Solitaire tips

- **Turn up hidden cards first.** Moves that reveal a face-down card are almost always the best — especially in the columns with the most hidden cards.
- **Don’t empty a column without a king to fill it.** An empty column only takes a king, so clear one when a king is waiting.
- **Think before playing from the waste.** It’s often better to free cards in the columns first and use the stock later.
- **Keep the colours balanced.** If you build a long red-black run, make sure the other colour of the next card is still reachable.
- **Don’t rush cards up.** A card on a foundation can’t hold the next lower card; keep useful cards in play until they are safe to move up.

#### About Klondike

Klondike is the best-known patience game, so well known in the US and Canada that “solitaire” on its own usually means Klondike; in the UK it is often just called patience. Where its name comes from is unknown — the late-1890s Klondike Gold Rush is a popular guess, but nothing proves it.

Its fame today owes a lot to Microsoft, which included Solitaire with Windows 3.0 in 1990, partly to teach people to use a mouse by dragging cards. Whether a random deal can be won is still an open question in mathematics; with every card known, about 82% of draw-three deals can be won, but nobody has worked out the exact figure for the real game, where most cards are hidden.

### FAQ

**Is every solitaire game winnable?**
No. Some deals can’t be won however well you play — even knowing where every card is, roughly one draw-three deal in five is impossible. With **Winnable deals only** on, the solver checks each deal before you play it, so every game here can be won.

**What is the difference between draw 1 and draw 3?**
In **Draw 1** you turn one card from the stock at a time, so you can reach every card — it’s easier. In **Draw 3** you turn three at a time and can only play the top one, so many cards stay buried; this is the classic, harder game.

**How does Vegas scoring work?**
You “pay” $52 for the deck and win $5 for each card you move to the foundations, so you need 11 cards to break even. You get one pass through the stock drawing one card, or three passes drawing three. Your running total is kept.

**How is the score calculated?**
Standard scoring follows Windows Solitaire: 10 points for a card to a foundation, 5 for playing from the waste to a column or turning over a card, −15 for moving a card back down, and −100 for turning the waste over when drawing one. Time takes 2 points every 10 seconds, and a win adds 700,000 ÷ your seconds.

**Can I play the same deal again or share it?**
Yes. **Restart** replays the current deal, and **Share this deal** gives a link with the game number, so a friend gets exactly the same cards.

**Does it save my game?**
Yes — your game in progress, settings and stats are saved in this browser. Close the tab and carry on later.

**Is it free?**
Yes, completely free with no download and no sign-up. It works on phones, tablets and computers.

- Remove the 144 tiles two at a time by matching **free** pairs — a tile is free when nothing lies on top of it and its left or right side is open. Any two **flowers** match, and so do any two **seasons**.

### Features

### How to play mahjong solitaire

1. **Find a free tile** — A tile is free if no tile lies on top of it and it can slide out to the left or right — one side must be open.
2. **Match a pair** — Tap two free tiles that are the same to remove them. Any flower matches any flower, and any season matches any season.
3. **Open up the board** — Prefer pairs that free the most tiles: the top of the stacks and the long rows’ ends.
4. **Use help when stuck** — Press **Hint** for a pair that keeps the game winnable, **Undo** to step back, or **Shuffle** when no pairs are left.
5. **Clear the board** — Remove all the tiles to win.

### Guide

#### The tiles

| Group | Tiles | How many |

#### Tips

- **Work from the top and the ends.** Tiles on top of stacks and at the ends of long rows hold the most other tiles in place.
- **When three of a kind are free, think first.** Removing the wrong two can leave the fourth stuck under its twin.
- **Clear long rows from both ends** so a single tile doesn’t end up blocking a whole row.
- **Save the flowers and seasons** — they match freely, so they’re handy when you need one more move.
- **All four of a kind free? Take them.** Removing a complete set can never hurt.

#### About mahjong solitaire

Mahjong solitaire uses the tiles of the four-player game mahjong, but it is a matching game for one. Brodie Lockard wrote the first computer version, *Mah-Jongg*, in 1981 on the PLATO system, and Activision’s *Shanghai* (1986) brought it to home computers. The classic starting arrangement is called the turtle.

### FAQ

**How do you play mahjong solitaire?**
Tap two matching tiles that are both free to remove them. A tile is free when nothing is on top of it and its left or right side is open. Clear all the tiles to win.

**Is every game winnable?**
Here, yes — each board is built by playing a game backwards, so it can always be cleared. With truly random deals, about 3% of turtle boards can never be cleared.

**Which tiles match?**
Identical tiles match. The exceptions are the flowers and the seasons: any flower matches any other flower, and any season matches any other season.

**What if there are no moves left?**
Press **Shuffle** to rearrange the remaining tiles in the same places — the new arrangement can still be cleared — or **Undo** to go back.

**What does the hint do?**
It asks a solver for a pair that keeps the board winnable and highlights it. If the board can no longer be cleared, it tells you so you can undo or shuffle.

**Can I play on my phone?**
Yes. The board fits phone screens; for bigger tiles, try the Pyramid or Quick layout or full screen.

### Guide

#### Repeated letters

A letter is coloured only as many times as it appears in the answer. If you guess GEESE and the answer is THOSE, only the final E turns green — the other two Es are grey, because THOSE has just one E. Exact matches are coloured first, then letters in the wrong spot from left to right.

#### Tips for solving in fewer guesses

- **Start with common letters.** Words with E, A, R, O, T, L, I, S and N give you the most information.
- **Use new letters early.** On your second guess, try mostly letters you haven’t used yet, even if you suspect a word.
- **Remember repeated letters.** Words like LEVEL, GEESE or APPLE trip people up — the answer can repeat a letter.
- **Think about word endings.** -ER, -LY, -ED and -ING patterns (in six letters) narrow things fast.
- **Save hard mode for later.** Normal mode lets you spend a guess on testing letters.

### Guide

#### How the pieces move

| Piece | Moves | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| King | One square any way; castling with a rook | — |
| Queen | Any distance along ranks, files and diagonals | 9 |
| Rook | Any distance along ranks and files | 5 |
| Bishop | Any distance along diagonals | 3 |
| Knight | An L: two squares one way, one square to the side; jumps over pieces | 3 |
| Pawn | One square forward (two from its first square); captures diagonally; promotes on the last rank | 1 |

#### Special rules

- **Castling**: the king moves two squares toward a rook, and the rook jumps to the other side. Not allowed if either has moved, if a square between them is occupied, or if the king is in check, passes through check or ends in check.
- **En passant**: when a pawn moves two squares and lands beside an enemy pawn, that pawn may capture it as if it had moved one square — but only on the very next move.
- **Promotion**: a pawn reaching the far rank becomes a queen, rook, bishop or knight.
- **Draws**: stalemate (no legal move but not in check), the same position three times, fifty moves each without a capture or pawn move, or not enough material left to checkmate.

Yes — choose **A friend** and take turns. Use **Flip** to turn the board.

To castle, move the king two squares toward the rook; the rook follows automatically. When a pawn reaches the last rank you choose its new piece (or switch on “Always promote to a queen”).

**What is PGN and FEN?**
PGN records a whole game move by move; FEN describes a single position. Copy either to use in other chess software, or paste a FEN under “Set up a position” to play from it.

Yes, your game in progress, settings and results are saved in this browser.

### How to play Spider Solitaire

2. **Keep runs in one suit** — A run of one suit (say 9-8-7 of hearts) can be moved together; mixed-suit runs can only be moved a card at a time.

4. **Deal when stuck** — Tap the stock to deal one card onto every column. You can’t deal while a column is empty.

### Guide

#### Difficulty levels

| Suits | Cards | What changes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 suit | 8 × spades | Every card can join any run — the gentle way to learn. |
| 2 suits | 4 × spades, 4 × hearts | Runs of two suits block each other; planning matters. |

#### Spider Solitaire tips

- **Turn up face-down cards** as early as you can — especially in the columns with the most of them.
- **Build in suit whenever you can.** A same-suit run can move as one; a mixed run is stuck.
- **Empty a column** and keep it for a while: it is the most powerful space on the table.
- **Put cards on kings and high cards** before low ones, so runs have room to grow.
- **Before dealing, tidy up** — a new row covers every column, so fix what you can first.

#### About Spider

Spider is a two-pack patience in which the ten columns are built down by rank and cleared one complete suit at a time. Microsoft added Spider Solitaire to Windows in the Microsoft Plus! 98 pack with one-, two- and four-suit versions; an earlier Windows 3.x version was written in 1991 by John A. Junod. Hoyle’s Rules of Games puts the chance of winning the classic game with good play at about one in three.

### FAQ

**How do you play Spider Solitaire?**
Build the ten columns down in rank — any card on one a rank higher — and move runs of one suit together. When a column holds a full king-to-ace run of one suit, it is removed. Clear all eight runs to win; deal from the stock when you run out of moves.

**Which is easiest: 1, 2 or 4 suits?**
One suit is by far the easiest, because every run is in suit and can move as a group. Two suits is a good middle step, and four suits is the classic, hardest game.

**Why can’t I deal new cards?**
The rules don’t allow dealing while any column is empty. Move a card or run into the empty column first.

**How is the score worked out?**
As in Windows: you start with 500 points, lose 1 for every move or undo, and gain 100 for each suit you complete.

**Can every game be won?**
No. Most one-suit games can be won, but in the four-suit game only about one in three is won even with good play.

**Does it save my game?**
Yes — your game in progress, settings and stats are saved in this browser.

## FreeCell

URL: https://justtools.online/games/freecell/
Category: Games
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-21

Play FreeCell solitaire online free with the same numbered deals as Microsoft FreeCell (1 to 1,000,000). Hints, undo, a solver and stats. No sign-up.

### At a glance

- All **52 cards are dealt face up** into eight columns (four of seven, four of six). Four **free cells** each hold one card; the **foundations** build up by suit from the ace.
- Columns build down in **alternating colours**. Runs move together through the free cells and empty columns: up to **(free cells + 1) × 2 to the power of empty columns** cards at once.
- Deals use **Microsoft FreeCell’s numbering**, 1 to 1,000,000 — type a number to play the same game as on Windows. Game **#11982** is the only one of the original 32,000 that can’t be won.
- Almost every deal can be won: one 2018 study found just one impossible deal in about **84,000**. A built-in solver gives **hints** and can **solve the game for you**.
- **Tap a card** to send it to its foundation, a column or a free cell, or drag runs. Safe cards go up by themselves; **undo** has no limit.
- Paul Alfille created FreeCell on the PLATO system in **1978**. Stats, streaks, shareable deals and your game in progress are saved on this device — free, no sign-up.

### Features

- **Microsoft-numbered deals**: Game #1 here is game #1 on Windows — play famous deals or share any game by its number.
- **Smart moves**: Tap a card and it goes to the best place; runs move in one go, as many as the free cells allow.
- **A solver that helps**: Hints come from a real search, and it tells you when a position can no longer be won.
- **Undo without limits**: Step back as far as you like and try another line.
- **Left- or right-handed**: Put the foundations on the side you prefer.
- **Streaks and stats**: Win rate, fastest win and your best streak, saved in your browser.

### How to play FreeCell

1. **Free the aces** — Move cards off the aces and twos so they can go up to the foundations, built by suit from ace to king.
2. **Build down in alternating colours** — Put a card on one a rank higher of the other colour — a black 7 on a red 8.
3. **Use the free cells** — Park any single card in one of the four free cells. Use them sparingly: each empty cell lets you move longer runs.
4. **Empty a column** — An empty column takes any card or run and doubles how many cards you can move together.
5. **Finish** — Win by moving all 52 cards to the foundations. Safe cards go up by themselves.

### Guide

#### How many cards can I move at once?

A “supermove” is a shortcut for moving the cards one at a time through the free cells and empty columns — the game does it for you, so you only drag the whole run.

| Free cells | Empty columns | Run you can move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | 0 | 5 cards |
| 3 | 0 | 4 cards |
| 2 | 1 | 6 cards (3 into the empty column) |
| 4 | 1 | 10 cards (5 into the empty column) |
| 0 | 0 | 1 card |

#### FreeCell tips

- **Look before you move.** Every card is visible, so plan where the low cards will go.
- **Keep free cells empty** as long as you can — each one adds a card to the runs you can move.
- **Aim for an empty column**; it is worth more than a free cell.
- **Dig out aces and twos first**, especially those deep in a column.
- **Don’t fill the last free cell** unless it wins you something right away.

#### About FreeCell

FreeCell grew out of Baker’s Game, which Martin Gardner described in Scientific American in 1968; Paul Alfille changed it to build in alternating colours and wrote the first computer version on the PLATO system in 1978. Microsoft’s version numbered its deals, and of the original 32,000 only game #11982 has no solution. Across billions of deals, about one in 84,000 can’t be won.

### FAQ

**Is every FreeCell game winnable?**
Almost. Of Microsoft’s original 32,000 deals only #11982 can’t be won, and a 2018 study of 8.6 billion deals found about one impossible deal in 84,000.

**Are these the same games as Microsoft FreeCell?**
Yes — the deals use the same numbering, so typing a game number gives the same layout as the Windows game.

**Why can’t I move a long run?**
You can only move as many cards as the free cells and empty columns allow: (free cells + 1) × 2 for each empty column. Free up a cell or a column and try again.

**What do the free cells do?**
Each of the four cells holds one card, to get it out of the way. They’re the key to FreeCell — and the fewer you use, the more freedom you keep.

**Can the computer solve it for me?**
Yes. **Solve it for me** plays out a winning line from where you are (that game won’t count in your stats), and **Hint** shows the next move of a winning line.

**Is it free?**
Yes, free with no download and no sign-up. Your game and stats are saved in your browser.

### How to play Ludo

| Safe squares | The four start squares and the four star squares |
| Finishing | Exact roll needed to reach home; getting a token home earns another roll |

#### Ludo tips

- **Get tokens out early** — having two or three on the board gives you choices with every roll.
- **Park on safe squares** when an opponent is within six squares behind you.

#### About Ludo

Ludo is a simplified form of Pachisi, the cross-and-circle race game of India. It was sold in England as Ludo from 1896 — the name is Latin for “I play” — and is still one of the most-played board games in India, where it is often played with star safe squares.

The four coloured start squares and the four star squares. A token on them can’t be captured.

2. **Climb ladders** — If you finish on the foot of a ladder, climb straight up to its top.
3. **Watch out for snakes** — If you finish on a snake’s head, slide down to its tail.
4. **Roll a six** — A six gives you another roll (you can turn this rule off).
5. **Reach 100** — The first player to reach square 100 wins. Choose what happens if you roll past it.

### Guide

#### The boards

| Board | Ladders | Snakes | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Classic | 7 | 8 | Everyday games — more snakes than ladders, as on old Indian boards |
| Easy climb | 10 | 5 | Young children and quick games |
| Snake pit | 6 | 10 | A long, nail-biting race |
| Random | 8 | 9 | Something new every game |

#### House rules for square 100

- **Bounce back** (the default): roll too high and you count up to 100 and back again — on 97, a 5 takes you to 98.
- **Stay put**: you need the exact number; if the roll is too high, you don’t move.
- **Still wins**: any roll that reaches 100 wins, which makes games shorter.
- A study in The Mathematical Gazette (1993) worked out game lengths this way, treating the board as a Markov chain — the same maths shows the average on each board here.

#### About Snakes and Ladders

Snakes and Ladders began in India as part of a family of dice board games that also includes Pachisi, the ancestor of Ludo. Known as Moksha Patam, it was a lesson in morals: ladders were virtues such as generosity and humility, snakes were vices such as anger and theft, and reaching the top meant liberation (moksha). The Jain version is called Gyan Chaupar.

The game reached England in the 1890s — the earliest known English version was registered in 1892 — and later the United States, where it is sold as Chutes and Ladders. In Hindi it is called Saanp Seedhi, in Telugu Vaikunthapali and in Tamil Parama Padam. The phrase “back to square one” is thought to come from it.

### FAQ

**Can I play Snakes and Ladders with the computer?**
Yes. Choose **Computer** and play Red against one to three computer players, who roll by themselves.

**Can I play with friends?**
Yes, on one device: choose **Friends (pass & play)** and two to four players take turns.

**What happens if you roll more than you need to reach 100?**
You choose: bounce back off 100 (the default), stay where you are, or win anyway.

**Do you need a six to start?**
Not by default — everyone starts off the board and moves straight away. Switch on **Need a six to start** for that house rule.

**How long does a game take?**
Each board shows the average number of rolls one player needs, worked out from the board and your rules — around 38 on the Classic board with bounce-back.

**Is my game saved?**
Yes — the game in progress and your record against the computer are saved in this browser.

#### About the memory game

Memory — also known as Concentration, Pairs or Pelmanism — is played with cards laid face down. Players turn over two at a time looking for matches, so it rewards attention and short-term memory. ## Keyboard Tester

URL: https://justtools.online/device-tests/keyboard-test/
Category: Device Tests
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Test your keyboard online: every key lights up when pressed, with full-size, tenkeyless, laptop and Mac layouts, rollover and key-chatter checks. No install.

### At a glance

- Every key **lights up while you hold it** and **turns green** once it has worked, so a dead key stands out at a glance.
- Drawings for **full-size**, **tenkeyless**, **laptop** and **Mac** keyboards, in **ANSI (US)** or **ISO (UK and Europe)** shape.
- Shows **how many keys register at once** (rollover) — press a handful together to check for ghosting.
- Flags **key chatter**: a key that types twice because it registers again within 30 ms of being let go — the usual sign of a worn or dirty switch.
- Lists each **key event** with its key, code, keyCode and location, and how long the key was held — handy for checking remapped keys and macros.
- Nothing you type is stored or sent anywhere. Works with USB, Bluetooth and laptop keyboards.

### Features

- **See every key**: A live drawing of your keyboard: held keys light up, tested keys stay green.
- **Four layouts**: Full size with number pad, tenkeyless, laptop and Mac, in ANSI or ISO shape.
- **Rollover and ghosting**: See the most keys registered at the same time.
- **Chatter detection**: Catches keys that double-type, the classic fault of worn mechanical switches.
- **Event details**: key, code, keyCode, location, modifiers and hold time for developers and remappers.
- **System keys too**: In full screen, Chrome and Edge can also catch Esc and the Windows key.

### How to test your keyboard

1. **Pick your keyboard** — Choose full size, tenkeyless, laptop or Mac, and ANSI or ISO, so the drawing matches.
2. **Press every key** — Go row by row. Each key should light up while held and stay green afterwards.
3. **Look for gaps** — A key that stays grey did not register. Press it again firmly, then check it in another program.
4. **Test several at once** — Hold down several keys together; **Most keys at once** shows how many the keyboard reports.

### Guide

#### What the results mean

| You see | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| A key stays grey | The key did not register. It may be broken, disabled, or a key the browser never sees (such as Fn). |
| A key turns amber | Possible chatter: it registered twice in a row within 30 ms. Clean or replace the switch. |
| A different key lights up | The keyboard layout in your system settings may not match the keyboard, or the key is remapped. |
| Few keys at once | Many keyboards register only 2–6 keys together; gaming keyboards usually allow many more (n-key rollover). |

#### Keys a browser cannot test

- **Fn** is handled inside the keyboard and never reaches the computer — test it by using it with another key, such as Fn + F2.
- **Windows key, Print Screen and media keys** may be taken by the operating system first. Use **Test system keys (full screen)** in Chrome or Edge.
- **Shortcuts such as Ctrl + W or Ctrl + T** are kept by the browser and can’t be blocked — avoid them while testing.
- On a **Mac**, a key let go while ⌘ is held sends no release, so the drawing lets go of all keys when ⌘ is released.
- Laptop **function keys** often control brightness or volume unless Fn is held (or **Fn Lock** is on).

#### Keyboard not working? Check these

- **Connection**: re-plug a USB keyboard or try another port; charge and re-pair a Bluetooth one.
- **Num Lock**: the number pad types numbers only when Num Lock is on.
- **Layout**: if keys type the wrong characters, check the input language or keyboard layout in your system settings.
- **Filter Keys / Sticky Keys** (Windows accessibility settings) can make keys slow or behave oddly.
- **Dirt**: crumbs under a key make it stick or double-type — turn the keyboard over and use compressed air.

### FAQ

**How do I test my keyboard online?**
Open this page and press each key. Every key lights up while you hold it and turns green once it has worked; keys that stay grey did not register.

**What is key rollover and ghosting?**
Rollover is how many keys a keyboard can register at once. Ghosting is when pressing several keys makes an extra, unpressed key appear — or some keys go missing. Hold several keys together and watch **Most keys at once**.

**What is key chatter?**
A key that types twice from one press. The switch bounces and sends a second press within a few milliseconds. The test marks such keys in amber.

**Why does the Fn key not light up?**
Fn is handled inside the keyboard itself and is never sent to the computer, so no website or program can see it.

**Can I test a laptop or Mac keyboard?**
Yes — choose **Laptop** or **Mac** for a matching drawing. Mac keys show their command, option and control names.

**Is what I type saved?**
No. Key presses are shown on this page only and are never stored or sent anywhere.

## Mouse Tester

URL: https://justtools.online/device-tests/mouse-test/
Category: Device Tests
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Test your mouse online: all buttons including back and forward, unwanted double clicks from a worn switch, the scroll wheel, clicks per second and polling rate.

### At a glance

- Tests **all five buttons** — left, right, middle (wheel click), **back** and **forward** — and lights them up on a mouse drawing.
- Catches **unwanted double clicks**: a second press less than 80 ms after the first (you can change the limit) is the classic sign of a worn switch.
- Counts **scroll wheel** steps up, down and sideways, and shows whether the wheel moves in lines or pixels.
- Measures the **polling rate** — how often the mouse reports its position: 125 Hz for office mice, 1000 Hz or more for gaming mice.
- Shows **clicks per second (CPS)** and the fastest gap between presses.
- The back and forward buttons are caught inside the test box, so they don’t leave the page. Nothing is uploaded.

### Features

- **Double-click checker**: Find the fault behind accidental double clicks, dropped drags and files that open by themselves.
- **Every button**: Left, right, middle, back and forward, with counts and the fastest gap for each.
- **Polling rate**: Move in circles to see the report rate in Hz and the nearest standard rate.
- **Scroll wheel**: Counts each step both ways and sideways, to catch a wheel that skips or jumps back.
- **Clicks per second**: Live CPS and your best burst.
- **Movement trail**: See the pointer’s path to spot jumps, stutters and a dirty sensor.

### How to test your mouse

1. **Click each button** — Click the left, right and middle buttons, and the side buttons, inside the box. Each one lights up and counts.
2. **Check for double clicks** — Click the left button normally twenty or thirty times. Any press flagged as a double click means the switch is bouncing.
3. **Roll the wheel** — Scroll slowly up and down. Every step should count in the right direction.
4. **Measure the polling rate** — Move the mouse quickly in circles inside the box and read the rate in Hz.

### Guide

#### Why does my mouse double click by itself?

Inside each mouse button is a small metal spring switch. As it wears or oxidises, a single press can make contact twice within a few milliseconds — the computer sees a double click. It shows up as files opening when you meant to select them, drags that let go, or two shots instead of one in games.

The test flags any press that comes sooner after the previous one than a person can click on purpose. A few flags in a hundred clicks confirm the fault. Fixes: clean or replace the switch, use the warranty, or as a stopgap raise the double-click speed setting.

#### Polling rates

| Rate | Report every | Typical mouse |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 125 Hz | 8 ms | Office and older mice |
| 500 Hz | 2 ms | Mid-range gaming mice |
| 1000 Hz | 1 ms | Most gaming mice |
| 4000–8000 Hz | 0.25–0.125 ms | High-end esports mice (may need a special receiver) |

#### Mouse not working properly? Check these

- **Cursor jumps or stutters**: clean the sensor window underneath, and use a mouse mat — glass and glossy desks confuse optical sensors.
- **Wireless lag**: charge or replace the battery, and move the receiver closer (a USB extension cable helps).
- **Side buttons do nothing**: some mice need their own software to map them, or they are assigned to other actions.
- **Scroll wheel jumps back**: the wheel’s encoder is dirty or worn; compressed air sometimes helps.

### FAQ

**How do I do a mouse double click test?**
Click the left button normally many times inside the box. If the test reports unwanted double clicks, your switch registered two presses from one click.

**What is a good polling rate?**
1000 Hz (once every millisecond) is standard for gaming; 125 Hz is fine for office work. Higher rates use a little more processor time.

**Will the back button leave this page?**
Not when you press it inside the test box — the test catches it there. Outside the box it works as normal.

**Why does the polling rate read lower than my mouse’s setting?**
Some browsers group movement events, and the rate is only reached while the mouse moves fast. Use Chrome or Edge and move in quick circles.

**Can I test a laptop touchpad?**
Yes — taps, two-finger clicks and two-finger scrolling all register in the box.

**Is anything recorded?**
No. Clicks and movements are counted on this page only.

## Speaker Test

URL: https://justtools.online/device-tests/speaker-test/
Category: Device Tests
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Test your speakers and headphones online: left and right channels, surround, a 20 Hz – 20 kHz sweep, a tone generator and a phase (wiring) test. No install.

### At a glance

- Plays a chime or noise on the **left**, the **right**, **both**, or **moving from left to right**, so you can hear whether the channels are the right way round.
- If the browser reports **5.1 or 7.1 output**, each surround speaker and the subwoofer can be tested on its own.
- A **frequency sweep** glides from 20 Hz to 20 kHz (or just the bass or treble) and shows the frequency and musical note as it plays.
- Press **I can’t hear it any more** to see where your speakers — or your ears — stop at the top.
- A **tone generator** from 20 Hz to 20 kHz with sine, triangle, square and sawtooth waves, for finding rattles and testing a subwoofer.
- A **phase test** tells you whether one speaker’s + and − wires are swapped. All sound is made in your browser.

### Features

- **Left and right**: Separate test sounds for each channel, both together, and a sweep across.
- **Surround channels**: Front, centre, subwoofer and rear speakers on 5.1 and 7.1 systems.
- **Frequency sweep**: Full range, bass-only and treble-only sweeps with a live readout.
- **Tone generator**: Any frequency, four wave shapes and handy presets from 30 Hz to 17.4 kHz.
- **Phase test**: Find reversed speaker wiring by ear in seconds.
- **Safe volume**: Starts quietly, with a volume control and a Stop button always in reach.

### How to test your speakers

1. **Set a safe volume** — Turn your system volume low first, especially with headphones.
2. **Test left and right** — Press **Left**, then **Right**. Each sound should come only from that side.
3. **Run a sweep** — Press **Full range** and listen as the tone rises. Note where it starts and where it fades away.
4. **Check the bass** — Use **Bass 20 – 200 Hz** or a 30–50 Hz tone to hear your subwoofer and find rattles.
5. **Check the wiring** — With two speakers, compare **In phase** and **Out of phase** — in phase should sound fuller.

### Guide

#### What to listen for

| Test | Good result | If not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Left / Right | Sound only from the named side | Swap the cables, or check the balance setting in your sound settings |
| Both | Sound seems to come from the middle | One speaker is louder, or the balance is off |
| Bass sweep | Smooth rise with no buzzing | A rattle at one pitch means something loose nearby, or a damaged cone |
| Treble sweep | Clear up to about 15–17 kHz | Small speakers often fade early; headphones go higher |
| Phase | In phase sounds fuller and centred | Swap + and − on one speaker |

#### About frequencies

People hear roughly from 20 Hz (deep rumble) to 20 kHz (a faint hiss), and the top end drops with age — many adults stop hearing above 15–17 kHz. Small laptop and phone speakers rarely reproduce much below 100–150 Hz, so a bass sweep may stay silent until it reaches that point. This is a check of your sound system, not a hearing test.

#### No sound? Check these

- **Output device**: make sure the right speakers or headphones are selected in your system’s sound settings.
- **Mute and volume**: check the system volume, the browser tab (it may be muted), and the speakers’ own volume knob.
- **Bluetooth**: headphones in “hands-free” mode sound poor and may be mono — choose the stereo (A2DP) device.
- **Surround**: set the speaker configuration (5.1 or 7.1) in your sound settings, then reload this page.

### FAQ

**How do I test left and right speakers?**
Press **Left** and then **Right**. The chime should come only from that side. If it comes from the other side, the cables or headphones are swapped.

**Can I test 5.1 or 7.1 surround sound?**
Yes, when your browser reports more than two output channels. Each speaker then gets its own button, including the subwoofer.

**What frequency range should my speakers play?**
Good headphones cover about 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Laptop speakers often start around 150 Hz; bookshelf speakers around 50 Hz; a subwoofer goes down to 20–30 Hz.

**Is this a hearing test?**
No. It shows where your speakers and ears stop together. If you are worried about your hearing, see a professional.

**What does the phase test do?**
It plays the same bass on both speakers, then with one speaker flipped. If the flipped version sounds fuller, one speaker is wired + to −.

**Is anything recorded?**
No. The sounds are generated in your browser and nothing is recorded or uploaded.

## Dead Pixel Test

URL: https://justtools.online/device-tests/dead-pixel-test/
Category: Device Tests
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Find dead and stuck pixels with full-screen colour tests, check backlight bleed and banding, try the stuck pixel fixer and see your refresh rate and resolution.

### At a glance

- **Full-screen solid colours** — black, white, red, green, blue, cyan, magenta, yellow and grey — make faulty pixels stand out.
- **Black** reveals stuck (lit) pixels and **backlight bleed**; **white** reveals dead (black) pixels and dust.
- A **gradient** checks for colour banding, and **single-pixel patterns** check sharpness and scaling.
- A **stuck pixel fixer** flashes rapid colours over a small square or the whole screen — with a clear warning for people sensitive to flashing light.
- Shows your screen’s **real resolution**, aspect ratio, scaling, **refresh rate** (60, 120, 144 Hz…), colour depth and HDR support, plus a **pixels-per-inch** calculator.
- Works on monitors, laptops, TVs, tablets and phones. Nothing is uploaded.

### Features

- **Twelve test screens**: Nine solid colours, a gradient, a pixel grid and a sharpness pattern.
- **Quick to use**: Click, tap or press the arrow keys to move between screens; Esc to finish.
- **Stuck pixel fixer**: Rapid colour flashing over a draggable square or the whole screen.
- **Refresh rate**: Measured from how often the browser draws, snapped to the usual rates.
- **Screen facts**: Resolution, aspect ratio, scaling, colour depth, colour gamut and HDR.
- **Pixels per inch**: Enter the screen size to see how sharp it is.

### How to check a screen for dead pixels

1. **Clean the screen** — Wipe it with a dry microfibre cloth, so dust isn’t mistaken for a pixel.
2. **Start the test** — Press **Start full-screen test**. The screen turns black.
3. **Go through the colours** — Click or press → for each colour. Look over the whole screen from about 30 cm away.
4. **Note what you find** — A dot that’s always black is dead; a dot stuck on one colour is stuck. Note where it is for a warranty claim.

### Guide

#### Dead, stuck or hot pixel?

| You see | Name | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A black dot on white and colours | Dead pixel | The pixel gets no power. It usually can’t be fixed. |
| A red, green or blue dot on black or other colours | Stuck pixel | One of its parts stays on. Sometimes freed by the stuck pixel fixer or gentle pressure. |
| A white dot on black | Hot pixel | All parts stuck on. Treated like a stuck pixel. |
| Light glowing in from edges on black | Backlight bleed | Normal in small amounts on LCD screens; OLED screens don’t have it. |

#### Before you return a screen

- **Check the return window**: many shops accept returns for any reason for a short time — test a new screen on day one.
- **Read the pixel policy**: manufacturers often allow a few faulty pixels before a replacement is due, so count them and note where they are.
- **Take a photo** of the fault on a solid colour for your claim.
- **OLED burn-in** shows as faint shapes on the grey screen — common on phones with always-on bars.

### FAQ

**How do I test for dead pixels?**
Press **Start full-screen test** and go through each colour. A dot that doesn’t match the colour is a faulty pixel: black on every colour means dead, a fixed colour means stuck.

**Can a dead pixel be fixed?**
A truly dead pixel usually can’t. A stuck pixel sometimes recovers after 10–20 minutes of the stuck pixel fixer, or gentle pressure with a soft cloth (at your own risk).

**Is the stuck pixel fixer safe?**
It flashes rapidly, so don’t use it if you or anyone nearby may be sensitive to flashing light. Don’t watch it; cover the rest of the screen or leave the room while it runs.

**How accurate is the refresh rate?**
It is measured from how often the browser draws the page, which normally matches the screen. Battery saving or a busy computer can make it read lower.

**Does it work on phones and TVs?**
Yes. On an iPhone the page fills the browser window instead of going truly full screen — hide the toolbars by scrolling, or use landscape.

**Is anything uploaded?**
No. Everything happens on your screen; nothing is sent anywhere.

## Gamepad Tester

URL: https://justtools.online/device-tests/gamepad-test/
Category: Device Tests
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Test a game controller online: every button and trigger, both sticks with drift and circularity checks, vibration and raw values. Xbox, PlayStation, Switch Pro.

### At a glance

- Shows a **live controller**: buttons light up, **triggers fill** as you press them, and both **sticks** move on screen.
- Uses the names on **your** controller — A B X Y for Xbox, Cross Circle Square Triangle for PlayStation, B A Y X for Nintendo.
- Checks **stick drift**: leave the sticks alone and it shows how far off centre each one rests, against an 8% deadzone.
- Measures **circularity**: roll each stick around its edge and see how close to a circle it traces.
- Tests **vibration** — light and strong motors, and trigger rumble on controllers that have it (Chrome and Edge).
- Lists every **button and axis value**, the controller’s maker and IDs, and how often it updates. Works with several controllers at once.

### Features

- **Live controller drawing**: Buttons, D-pad, bumpers, triggers and sticks react as you press them.
- **Stick drift check**: Measures where each stick settles when you let go.
- **Circularity test**: Traces the stick’s edge to spot worn or badly calibrated sticks.
- **Vibration test**: Run each rumble motor, and the trigger motors on Xbox controllers.
- **Raw values**: Every button value and axis to three decimals, for remapping and debugging.
- **Several controllers**: Switch between connected controllers with one tap.

### How to test a controller

1. **Connect it** — Plug the controller in by USB or pair it by Bluetooth, then **press any button** — browsers only show a controller after a button press.
2. **Press every button** — Each one should light up on the drawing and in the Buttons list. Pull the triggers slowly — the bar should fill smoothly.
3. **Check for drift** — Let go of both sticks. The dot should settle inside the amber ring.
4. **Check circularity** — Roll each stick slowly around its outer edge a couple of times. The traced shape should be close to a circle.
5. **Test vibration** — Press **Light motor**, **Strong motor** and **Both** and feel for each.

### Guide

#### What is stick drift?

Drift is when a stick reports movement while you aren’t touching it — your character walks or the camera turns on its own. It is caused by wear or dirt in the stick’s sensors, and is common on older controllers.

Games ignore tiny movements inside a “deadzone” around the centre. If the resting dot stays inside the amber 8% ring, a normal deadzone hides it; if it rests outside, you will feel the drift in games. Cleaning, recalibrating, a larger deadzone in the game’s settings, or replacing the stick module are the fixes.

#### Circularity

| Error | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Under 10% | A round, well-calibrated stick. |
| 10–15% | Typical for many controllers; fine for most games. |
| Over 15% | A squarish or uneven gate, or a stick that doesn’t reach the edge in some directions. Diagonal movement may feel off. |

#### Controller not showing up?

- **Press a button** while this page is open — browsers hide controllers until then.
- **Use a data cable**: some USB cables only charge.
- **Bluetooth**: pair the controller in your system settings first (hold the pairing button until the light flashes).
- **Steam or other remapping apps** can take over the controller — close them and try again.
- **PlayStation and Nintendo controllers** work best in Chrome or Edge; Firefox may show them without the standard layout.

### FAQ

**How do I test my controller online?**
Connect it, press any button with this page open, then press every button and move both sticks. Everything that works lights up on the drawing.

**How do I check for stick drift?**
Let go of the sticks and watch the red dot in each stick box. If it rests outside the amber ring, the stick drifts.

**Does it work with PS5, PS4, Xbox and Switch Pro controllers?**
Yes — any controller your browser can see. Button names match the brand when the controller is recognised.

**Why can’t I test vibration?**
Vibration from a web page works in Chrome and Edge with most controllers. Firefox and Safari don’t support it yet.

**What is a good circularity error?**
Under about 10% is very good; 10–15% is typical. Higher values mean the stick doesn’t trace an even circle.

**Is anything sent anywhere?**
No. The controller is read inside your browser only.

## What Is My IP

URL: https://justtools.online/network-tools/what-is-my-ip/
Category: Internet & Network Tools
Processing: Contacts an external service to work (see the page).
Last updated: 2026-10-22

See your public IP address (IPv4 and IPv6), internet provider, approximate location and browser details — and check whether WebRTC leaks your IP past a VPN.

### At a glance

- Shows your **public IP address** the moment the page opens — the address websites see — with one-click copy.
- Both **IPv4 and IPv6**, so you can see whether your connection uses IPv6.
- Your **internet provider** (and its AS number) and an **approximate location** — usually your provider’s nearest city, not your home.
- A **WebRTC leak test** for VPN users, and a **time zone check** that shows when your device and IP disagree.
- Your **browser, system, screen and user agent**, handy when support asks “what are you using?”.
- **Hide IP for screenshots** masks the address. The IP comes from ipify and Cloudflare; nothing is stored by JustTools.

### Features

- **Instant IP**: Your public IPv4 and IPv6 addresses with copy buttons.
- **Provider and place**: Internet provider, AS number, city, country and time zone.
- **VPN leak test**: Checks whether WebRTC reveals a different public address.
- **Browser details**: Browser, system, device type, screen, language and user agent.
- **Screenshot-safe**: Hide the address with one tap before sharing a screenshot.
- **Who owns it**: Jump to a whois lookup of your IP for the network owner and range.

### How to find your IP address

1. **Open this page** — Your public IP address appears at the top straight away.
2. **Copy it** — Press the copy button next to the address you need — IPv4 for most purposes.
3. **Check a VPN** — With your VPN on, check that the address and location have changed, then run the WebRTC leak test.

### Guide

#### Public and private IP addresses

Your **public IP** is the address the internet sees; it belongs to your router or your mobile provider and is shared by every device on the same connection. Inside your home, each device has a **private IP** (such as 192.168.1.5) that only your router knows — find it in your device’s Wi-Fi settings.

Many mobile and some broadband providers in India and elsewhere use **carrier-grade NAT**, so hundreds of customers share one public IPv4 address. IPv6 avoids this: each device can have its own public address.

#### IPv4 and IPv6

|  | IPv4 | IPv6 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Looks like | 14.194.35.210 | 2401:4900:1c5a::1 |
| Number of addresses | About 4.3 billion | 340 undecillion |
| Shared between users | Often (NAT) | Rarely |

#### How accurate is IP location?

IP location is a guess from databases of which provider uses which addresses where. The country is almost always right; the city is often your provider’s nearest hub, which can be tens of kilometres away. It never shows your street or house, and a VPN shows the VPN server’s location instead.

### FAQ

**What is my IP address?**
It is shown at the top of this page: your public IP address, which every website you visit sees. Copy it with the button beside it.

**Why do I have two IP addresses?**
One is IPv4 (four numbers) and one is IPv6 (longer, with colons). Many connections now use both; websites that support IPv6 see that one.

**Why does my IP show the wrong city?**
IP location shows where your provider’s equipment is registered, not where you are. Mobile data especially can show a city far away.

**How do I check if my VPN is working?**
Turn the VPN on and reload: the IP, provider and location should change to the VPN’s. Then run the WebRTC leak test — it should not find your real address.

**Does my IP address change?**
Often, yes. Most home and mobile connections get a new public IP from time to time or when the router restarts, unless you pay for a static IP.

**Is it safe to share my IP?**
It reveals your rough location and provider, not your identity. Avoid posting it publicly anyway — use **Hide IP for screenshots**.

## Whois Lookup

URL: https://justtools.online/network-tools/whois-lookup/
Category: Internet & Network Tools
Processing: Contacts an external service to work (see the page).
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Free whois lookup for any domain, IP address or AS number: registrar, registration and expiry dates, name servers, owner, network range and abuse contact.

### At a glance

- Looks up **domains**, **IP addresses** (IPv4 and IPv6, or a whole prefix) and **AS numbers** — paste a URL or an email address and it finds the domain.
- For domains: the **registrar**, **registration date and age**, **expiry date** and days left, last update, **name servers**, **DNSSEC** and every **status lock** explained in plain English.
- For IP addresses and networks: the **owner**, address **range and CIDR**, country, network type and the regional registry (ARIN, RIPE, APNIC, LACNIC or AFRINIC).
- Shows the **abuse contact** — the right place to report spam, phishing or attacks.
- Uses **RDAP**, the modern, structured replacement for WHOIS that ICANN requires of every registry and registrar. The query goes through rdap.org to the registry itself.
- If a domain isn’t registered, it says so — the name may be available. Free, no sign-up, no captcha.

### Features

- **Domains, IPs and ASNs**: One box for all three, from a URL, email address or plain name.
- **Expiry and age**: See when a domain was registered, how old it is and how many days are left.
- **Status locks explained**: Codes such as clientTransferProhibited in plain words.
- **Registrar detail**: Also asks the registrar’s own RDAP server for the registrant’s region and abuse contacts.
- **Network owners**: Range, CIDR and owner of any IP, from the regional internet registry.
- **Raw data**: The full RDAP response, and a one-click summary to copy.

### How to look up who owns a domain or IP

1. **Type or paste** — Enter a domain (example.com), a web address, an IP address (8.8.8.8) or an AS number (AS15169).
2. **Look up** — Press **Look up**. The tool asks the registry responsible for that name or address.
3. **Read the summary** — Check the registrar, dates, name servers, owner and status — or open the raw response.
4. **Report abuse** — To report spam or phishing, use the abuse contact shown.

### Guide

#### Why is the owner “redacted for privacy”?

Since the EU’s GDPR came into force in 2018, registrars hide the personal details of most domain owners. You usually see only the owner’s state or country. To contact an owner, use the contact form or email relay the registrar links to, or ask the registrar. Company-owned IP networks still show the organisation’s name.

#### WHOIS and RDAP

WHOIS is the old text-based way of asking who registered a domain; every registry formatted its answers differently. RDAP (Registration Data Access Protocol) replaces it with the same information as structured data, over HTTPS. ICANN made RDAP mandatory for generic top-level domains, and the regional internet registries use it for IP addresses and AS numbers. Some country-code domains don’t offer RDAP yet.

#### Common domain status codes

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| clientTransferProhibited | Locked against transfer to another registrar — a normal safety setting. |
| clientHold / serverHold | The domain has been taken off the internet, often for non-payment or a dispute. |
| redemptionPeriod | Expired and deleted; the previous owner can still restore it for a fee. |
| pendingDelete | About to be deleted, after which anyone may register it. |
| ok / active | No locks or pending actions. |

### FAQ

**How do I find out who owns a domain?**
Enter the domain and press **Look up**. You’ll see the registrar and, unless it is redacted for privacy, the owner. Most personal owners are hidden since 2018 — contact them through the registrar.

**How can I check when a domain expires?**
Look it up: the **Expires** box shows the date and how many days are left. A domain that has expired may show a redemption or pending-delete status.

**Is the domain available?**
If the registry has no record, the tool says so and the name may be available. Confirm with a registrar — some names are reserved or sold as premium.

**Can I look up an IP address?**
Yes. You’ll see which organisation the address block belongs to, its range and CIDR, country and the abuse contact.

**What is an AS number?**
An Autonomous System number identifies a network on the internet, such as an internet provider or a cloud company (Google is AS15169).

**Where does the data come from?**
From the registries’ RDAP services, reached through rdap.org. Only what you type is sent; JustTools doesn’t keep it.

## MAC Address Lookup

URL: https://justtools.online/network-tools/mac-address-lookup/
Category: Internet & Network Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Look up the maker of any MAC address from the official IEEE list, in bulk too. Spots random private addresses, converts formats and generates MACs.

### At a glance

- Finds the **maker** of a MAC address from the **IEEE registry** — over 54,000 assigned blocks, including the smaller MA-M and MA-S blocks.
- Paste **one address or hundreds** (one per line) — in any format: AA:BB:CC…, aa-bb-cc…, aabb.ccdd.eeff or plain.
- Explains **random “private” addresses** that phones and laptops use on Wi-Fi, and **multicast** and **broadcast** addresses.
- Shows the address in **other formats** with copy buttons, and the **IPv6 interface ID and link-local address** it would make.
- A **generator** makes random addresses for virtual machines and testing, or addresses under a chosen maker prefix.
- Works on your device: the vendor list loads once and the addresses you type are never sent anywhere.

### Features

- **Official IEEE data**: MA-L, MA-M and MA-S assignments, most specific match first.
- **Bulk lookup**: Check a whole router client list or ARP table at once.
- **Private addresses explained**: Recognises randomised Wi-Fi addresses that hide the maker.
- **Any format**: Colons, hyphens, Cisco dots or none — converted for you.
- **IPv6 link-local**: The modified EUI-64 interface ID a MAC produces.
- **MAC generator**: Random, locally administered unicast addresses, or under a maker’s prefix.

### How to look up a MAC address

1. **Copy the address** — Find it in your router’s device list, or in the device’s network settings.
2. **Paste it** — Paste one address, or a list with one per line.
3. **Look up** — Press **Look up** to see the maker, its country and the registry block.

### Guide

#### How to find a device’s MAC address

| Device | Where to look |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | Open Command Prompt and type ipconfig /all — “Physical Address”. |
| Mac | System Settings → Network → your connection → Details → Hardware. |
| iPhone / iPad | Settings → General → About → Wi-Fi Address (or the network’s “Private Wi-Fi Address”). |
| Android | Settings → About phone → Status (or Wi-Fi network details → MAC address). |
| Linux | Run ip link — the “link/ether” value. |
| Router | The list of connected devices in its web page or app. |

#### Why does my phone show an unknown maker?

Phones, tablets and Windows laptops now use a different random MAC address for each Wi-Fi network, so they can’t be tracked between networks. Such addresses have the “locally administered” bit set — the second digit is 2, 6, A or E — and belong to no maker. That is normal, and the lookup says so.

#### About the IEEE registry

The first half of a MAC address is an Organizationally Unique Identifier (OUI) that the IEEE Registration Authority assigns to manufacturers. Large blocks (MA-L) cover 16.7 million addresses; smaller MA-M and MA-S blocks go to smaller makers. Some companies pay to keep their name private, shown here as “Private”.

### FAQ

**What does a MAC address lookup tell me?**
Which company the network chip’s address block was assigned to — usually the device maker (or the maker of its Wi-Fi chip).

**Can I find a person or location from a MAC address?**
No. A MAC address identifies a network chip’s maker only. It isn’t sent over the internet beyond your local network.

**Why is the vendor unknown?**
Either the address is a random private address (common on phones), or the block was assigned recently. The tool tells you which.

**Can I look up many MAC addresses at once?**
Yes — paste up to 500, one per line.

**Is it safe to generate a random MAC?**
Yes, for virtual machines and testing. Generated addresses are locally administered and unicast, so they won’t clash with real devices’ factory addresses.

**Are the addresses I enter uploaded?**
No. The vendor list is downloaded to your browser and the lookup happens there.

## Ping Test

URL: https://justtools.online/network-tools/ping-test/
Category: Internet & Network Tools
Processing: Contacts an external service to work (see the page).
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Free online ping test: measure ping, jitter and packet loss from your device to 31 data centres worldwide — India, Asia, Europe, the US and more — in seconds.

### At a glance

- Measures the **round-trip time (ping)** from your device to **31 Amazon Web Services data centres** — Mumbai, Hyderabad, Singapore, Dubai, Frankfurt, London, Virginia, São Paulo, Sydney and more — and your **nearest Cloudflare server**.
- Shows the **median** and **best** ping, **jitter** (how much it varies) and **packet loss** for each place.
- Sorts the results so the **fastest data centre** comes first, and rates it for gaming and video calls.
- Each server gets a warm-up request first, so connection setup doesn’t inflate the result.
- Filter by region, choose 5 or 10 pings per server, and copy the results to share with support.
- Runs in your browser — no app. Browsers can’t send ICMP pings, so this times a tiny HTTPS request instead, which reads a few milliseconds higher.

### Features

- **31 data centres**: Across Asia, the Middle East, Europe, Africa, the Americas and Australia.
- **Jitter and packet loss**: Not just the average — the steadiness that games and calls need.
- **Fastest first**: Results sorted by ping, with a plain rating.
- **Nearest server baseline**: Your ping to Cloudflare’s closest server — about as low as it gets.
- **Region filter**: Test only the part of the world you care about.
- **Copy results**: A neat text summary for forums, support tickets or your ISP.

### How to test your ping

1. **Close downloads** — Pause downloads, streams and updates on your network for a fair result.
2. **Start the test** — Press **Start ping test**. Each data centre is pinged several times.
3. **Read the results** — Look at the median ping for the places you play or call, plus jitter and loss.

### Guide

#### What is a good ping?

| Ping | Rating | Feels like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Under 50 ms | Excellent | Instant — ideal for competitive games |
| 50–100 ms | Good | Fine for most games and video calls |
| 100–180 ms | Fair | Noticeable in fast shooters; calls still OK |
| Over 180 ms | High | Lag in games, talk-over in calls |

#### Ping, jitter and packet loss

- **Ping (latency)** is the time for a message to reach a server and come back. Distance matters: light in fibre covers roughly 200 km per millisecond, so Mumbai to Frankfurt can’t be much under 100 ms.
- **Jitter** is how much the ping changes from one moment to the next. Below 10 ms is good; high jitter makes calls choppy.
- **Packet loss** means some messages never arrive. Anything above 1–2% causes stutters and dropped audio.

#### How to lower your ping

- Use a **wired (Ethernet) connection** instead of Wi-Fi, or move closer to the router.
- Stop **downloads, uploads and streaming** on other devices while you play.
- Pick **game servers in the nearest region** — the table shows which is fastest for you.
- Restart your router, and ask your provider about congestion if evening pings are much higher.

### FAQ

**What does a ping test measure?**
How long a small message takes to travel from your device to a server and back, in milliseconds — plus how steady that is (jitter) and whether any messages get lost.

**Why is my ping higher here than in the command line?**
Browsers can’t send ICMP ping packets, so this test times a tiny HTTPS request on an open connection. That adds a few milliseconds of processing.

**Which servers are tested?**
Amazon Web Services data centres in 31 cities (the same regions many games and apps run in) and Cloudflare’s server nearest to you.

**Is this the ping to my game?**
It is a good guide: games hosted on AWS in the same region will be close. Game servers elsewhere may differ.

**Does the test use much data?**
No — each ping is a few hundred bytes, under 100 KB for the whole test.

**Is anything stored?**
No. The servers see your IP address like any website does; results stay in your browser.

## Image to Text (OCR)

URL: https://justtools.online/image-tools/image-to-text/
Category: Image Tools
Processing: Runs entirely in the browser; user data is not uploaded.
Last updated: 2026-10-22

Extract text from images, screenshots and scanned pages online, free. 32 languages incl. Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and Bengali. Your image stays on your device.

### At a glance

- **Reads the text in any image** — photos of notes and books, screenshots, scanned pages, receipts, posters — and gives you text to **copy, edit or download**.
- **32 languages**: English, **Hindi**, Marathi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Punjabi, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, Urdu, Sanskrit, plus Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, French and more. Mix up to three, such as Hindi + English.
- **Several images at once** — drop them in, or paste a screenshot with **Ctrl + V**. JPG, PNG, WebP and iPhone HEIC photos all work.

### Features

- **Indian languages**: Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Punjabi, Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, Urdu and Sanskrit.
- **Private**: OCR runs on your device; your images stay with you.
- **Batch and paste**: Many images at once, or paste a screenshot straight from the clipboard.
- **Clean text**: Keep the original lines or join them into paragraphs; hyphenated words are mended.
- **See what’s unsure**: Low-confidence words are highlighted on the image so you know what to check.
- **Copy or download**: Edit the text, copy it, or save it as a .txt file.

### How to convert an image to text

1. **Choose the language** — Tap the language of the text — for example **Hindi**, or **Hindi + English** for mixed text.
2. **Add the image** — Drop a photo or screenshot on the box, click to choose one, or press **Ctrl + V** to paste.
3. **Wait a moment** — The first time, the language file downloads. Then the text appears beside the image.
4. **Check and copy** — Check the highlighted words, fix anything wrong, then press **Copy text** or download a .txt file.

### Guide

#### Tips for the best results

- **Choose the right language** — Hindi text read as English comes out as nonsense.
- **Sharp and straight**: hold the phone parallel to the page, in good light, without shadows.
- **Crop to the text** — a page full of pictures or tables confuses the reader.
- For **screenshots, posters and signs**, choose **Scattered text** under Reading options.
- **Handwriting** is hard for any OCR; neat print works best.

#### What is OCR?

OCR (optical character recognition) turns pictures of letters into real, editable text. This tool uses Tesseract, a free OCR engine first developed at Hewlett-Packard and later maintained with Google’s support, with its neural-network (LSTM) models. It runs here as WebAssembly inside your browser, so your images don’t go to any server.

### FAQ

**How do I extract text from an image?**
Choose the language, then drop the image on the box (or paste it with Ctrl + V). The text appears in a few seconds, ready to copy or download.

**Does it work with Hindi?**
Yes. Choose **Hindi** — or Hindi and English together for mixed text. Marathi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Punjabi and other Indian languages work too.

**Is my image uploaded?**
No. The text is read by an OCR engine running in your browser. Only the language file is downloaded (from the jsDelivr CDN) the first time you use a language.

**Can it read handwriting?**
Only very neat handwriting, and not reliably. It is designed for printed and typed text.

**Why are some words wrong?**
Blurry, small, curved or low-contrast text is hard to read. Use a sharper photo, keep **Enlarge small text** on, and check the words highlighted in orange.

**Can I convert several images at once?**
Yes — add up to 20 at a time, then copy them all or download them as one .txt file.

### Guide

#### Why does my bank give a different rate?

This converter shows the **mid-market rate** — the midpoint between the prices at which banks buy and sell a currency. Banks, card networks, money changers and remittance apps add a margin (often 1–4%) and sometimes a fixed fee. To compare offers, convert the amount here, then see how much less you actually receive.

| --- | --- |

| AED → INR, SAR → INR | Money sent home from the UAE and Saudi Arabia |
| GBP → INR, EUR → INR | Travel, tuition and family in the UK and Europe |
| INR → USD | Buying from US sites and paying for software |

#### Where the rates come from

Current rates come from ExchangeRate-API’s open access feed, which updates once a day. The history chart uses the European Central Bank’s daily reference rates (published on working days, around 16:00 Central European Time) through the Frankfurter service. Rates are for information only — always confirm with your bank or provider before you transfer money.

The European Central Bank, the source of the history, doesn’t publish rates for every currency. Current conversion still works for all 160.

Yes: +, −, ×, ÷, brackets and percentages, such as 2,500 × 12 or 1000 + 18%.

#### How the key points are found

The calculator samples every curve across the visible window, looks for places where it changes sign (a root), turns round (a maximum or minimum) or meets another curve, and then narrows each one down to about 12 significant digits. Jumps such as the one in 1/x at x = 0 are recognised as asymptotes, not roots. Zoom in or move the graph to find points outside the current view.

### FAQ

**Is this graphing calculator free?**

**How do I find where two graphs intersect?**
Enter both functions. Every crossing in view is marked with a dark dot and listed under the graph with its coordinates.

**How do I find the roots of an equation?**
Type the equation as y = (left side) − (right side). The roots are where the curve crosses the x-axis; they are marked and listed with their x values.

**Can it use degrees instead of radians?**
Yes. Switch Angles to Degrees, and sin(30) becomes 0.5. Inverse functions such as asin then answer in degrees too.

**Why does my graph have a gap?**
Some functions are undefined for some x — √x for negative x, ln x for x ≤ 0, or 1/x at 0. The calculator leaves those parts blank instead of drawing a wrong line.

**Can I save or share my graph?**
Download it as a PNG image, or copy a link that opens the same functions and view on any device. Your functions are also remembered in this browser.
